    The handbook · 17 November 2026

    The docenta handbook

    A complete guide, from an empty machine to a working private search engine over your whole digital life. No prior knowledge is assumed: every command is written out, every path is spelled out, and every step says what it does and how you know it worked.

    How to read this#

    Chapters 1 to 4take you from nothing to your first answer. Do them in order, once.Chapters 5 to 7are daily use: searching, bringing in mail and chats, keeping it fresh automatically.Chapters 8 to 13are the reference half: maintenance, upgrades, troubleshooting, the full command list, the pages docenta shows you, and the glossary. Come back to them as needed.

    Commands in this handbook are written for macOS and Linux shells. Windows notes appear where the two differ. Anything you type is shown like this:

    bash
    docenta status --content

    and the output that proves it worked is shown right after it.

    1. What docenta is#

    Docenta is a private search-and-memory engine for everything you own: every file on every drive, decades of email, and the conversations you have had with AI assistants. It runs entirely on your own machine. It has no network code at all, so nothing can leave, even by accident.

    Classic file search answers *"which files exist and where"*. Docenta answers *"which files contain this"*, and every answer comes with a citation that points at the exact passage it came from.

    The one design idea#

    Originals are never copied. Docenta reads your files and stores only *derived* searchable material: compressed text sidecars, a full-text index, and a small database mapping content back to paths. Your files stay exactly where they are, untouched. Everything docenta stores can be deleted and rebuilt from your files at any time.

    Identity is by content, not by path. Ten copies of the same document across ten drives cost one extraction and one index entry, and moving a file is a database row update rather than a re-index.

    Who it is for#

    The primary user is not a person typing in a search box: it is an AI agent working on your behalf. Docenta speaks MCP (Model Context Protocol), so Claude Code, Claude Desktop, or any MCP-capable local model can search everything you have indexed and quote it with proof. Everything the agent can do, you can also do yourself from the command line: the two surfaces return the same data.

    What it is not#

    • It is not a cloud service, and it has no accounts or sync-to-server.
    • It is not a file manager or a backup tool. It never modifies or moves your
      • files.
    • It is not a chatbot. It retrieves and proves; the reasoning is your agent's
      • job.

    2. Before you start#

    What you need#

    RequirementDetail
    Operating systemmacOS (Apple Silicon or Intel), Windows, or Linux. Behavior is identical on all three.
    Disk spaceBudget roughly 18 percent of the raw bytes you point it at - that is everything docenta puts on disk, models included. On the reference machine, 358 GB of files cost 64 GB all in. Text-heavy corpora run higher, photo and video libraries far lower: only text becomes an index. Chapter 8.3 has the measured breakdown.
    Memory8 GB works (docenta calls this the "constrained" profile and adapts). 16 GB or more runs everything without compromise.
    TimeIndexing a large collection of files runs for hours in the background the first time. You can search it while it builds.

    The two halves you will install#

    Docenta ships as two programs that work together:

    1. docenta - the engine. Finds files, extracts their text, indexes it,
      2. answers keyword searches, and serves the MCP tools to your agent. This half works with no models and no AI at all.
    2. docenta-semantic - the meaning layer. Adds semantic ("what I mean,
      3. not what I typed") search, the entity and timeline layers, and evidence packs. This half needs the ONNX runtime and the models, which onboarding fetches for you (chapter 3). You reach it as docenta layers <verb>, docenta cloud <verb> and docenta ask: one binary name to type. docenta starts the meaning layer's program from its own install, with the same output.

    You can stop after installing the first half and have a genuinely useful tool. The second half is what makes it feel like memory.

    A note on time and patience#

    Tip

    Docenta is built to be interrupted. Every stage writes its progress to a cursor on disk. If you close the laptop, kill the process, or lose power in the middle of a twelve-hour index, nothing is corrupted: the next run picks up where it stopped. You never need to start over.

    3. Installing docenta#

    docenta arrives ready to run. There is nothing to build, no compiler to install and no code to fetch: every program is compiled, signed and checked before it reaches you. Two commands do the whole job, and this chapter says exactly what each one does.

    3.1 Install the programs#

    macOS (Apple silicon or Intel) and Linux x64. One line in the terminal:

    bash
    curl -fsSL https://dl.docenta.ai/install.sh | DOCENTA_CHANNEL=family bash

    What that line does, and nothing else:

    1. It downloads the current build for your machine from dl.docenta.ai.
    2. It checks the download against a signed checksum list, using the docenta
      3. release key that is built into the script. A file that was changed or swapped on the way is refused.
    3. It places docenta, the one program you type, in ~/.docenta/bin, and
      4. the programs it starts in helpers below it; this handbook, the readme, the release notes, the licence and the completion scripts go into ~/.docenta/doc.
    4. It remembers which channel you installed from, for later updates, and
      5. prints the next command.

    It does not touch your shell configuration, asks for no password and installs nothing outside ~/.docenta.

    Windows 10 or 11, x64. One line in PowerShell (the one Windows ships is enough):

    powershell
    $env:DOCENTA_CHANNEL = "family"; irm https://dl.docenta.ai/install.ps1 | iex

    It does what the line above does, with what Windows carries: it downloads the build, checks the signed checksum list against the docenta release key built into the script (with the ssh-keygen of Windows' own OpenSSH client) and the download against that list, and refuses a file that was changed. It places docenta.exe in %LOCALAPPDATA%\docenta\bin, the programs it starts in helpers below it and the documents in %LOCALAPPDATA%\docenta\doc, remembers the channel, and puts that one folder on your user PATH when it is not there yet. It asks for no administrator rights. There is no package manager entry yet.

    The window you typed it in can type docenta at once; other windows see the folder when they are opened anew.

    Note

    On macOS and Linux, open a new terminal window after the install, or add the folder to your PATH in the current one: export PATH="$HOME/.docenta/bin:$PATH".

    Warning

    Keep the install folder as the installer left it. docenta is the one program you type; it finds the others beside itself or in the helpers folder below it, and moving one of them away breaks the part it does.

    3.2 Onboard: one command does the rest#

    bash
    docenta setup onboard

    First it asks how you want it to run: autopilot, where you answer every question now and it then runs through on its own, or step by step, where each phase is explained and confirmed by you before it starts. Either way, nothing long starts while a question is still open.

    Then, in order:

    1. It says where docenta will live (its store and its models) and how much
      2. room that volume has. When that volume is small and a roomier one is mounted, it lists the roomier volumes and asks which to use; a number picks one, a path is taken as written, Enter keeps the default. The choice is recorded in the config, so nothing lands on a full system disk.
    2. It fetches the ONNX Runtime and the models (about 3 GB, once).
    3. It sizes your machine and your files in a read-only walk.
    4. It asks the rest of its questions, every one now, before anything runs.
      5. The same questions stand on a page in your browser beside the terminal: the terminal prints the page's address and opens it, every question on the page starts not set with its default marked, nothing is chosen for you, and every toggle you make shows in the terminal as a line and is kept in a draft at once. Answer on the page and press its button (it points at any question still open and refuses until all are answered), or press Enter in the terminal to answer the open ones there, each with its default (Enter takes it); an answer typed in the terminal shows on the page, a click on the page answers the question the terminal is on, and when the terminal took part it shows the final selection and waits for your Enter before anything starts. The "answered" tag on a question unsets it again. --cli-only keeps everything in the terminal. The questions:
    • OCR - "N images and M documents would go through OCR": on runs
      • the text recognition over scanned PDFs and pictures in the background, and keeps running it: every update's produce step reads what arrived since, within its budget, until the answer changes; later (the default) leaves those files findable by name and metadata until you turn it on (docenta setup answers --set ocr=on).
    • Mail - connect a mail account (IMAP, kept fresh hourly): on the
      • page, now unfolds the whole mail setup under the question - the address this machine knows pre-filled, the provider's key steps, the app password typed once into the OS credential store - and the account is connected there and then (the question's note says connected: <address>; the terminal lists it); in the terminal, now runs docenta setup mail after the first scan; later (the default) prints the one line to run when you want it.
    • Agents - connect an AI agent: the page lists every agent found
      • on this machine (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, ChatGPT, each with where it was found) with a tick, so now connects the ticked ones after the build (none ticked: every one found, each shown and asked as docenta agents add does); later (the default) prints the one line. The transcript the agent sessions keep (full: every turn, tool call and result; prose: the conversation's words) is asked once here, beside the agents, for all of them; the per-agent word is docenta setup answers later.
    • Mailbox archives - asked only when a .mbox file is in scope,
      • with the count and the size: now explodes each archive into its messages after the scan (each message searchable on its own; a big archive is hours of work) and the hourly pass does the same for an archive that appears later; later (the default) records each archive by name and docenta ingest mailbox <file> explodes one when you want it. The archive file itself is captured like any other file at the explosion (its facts and access land on its row; the messages inside carry none by design, they are members, not files).
    1. It tells you how long the first build will take and how much disk it
      2. needs, and asks for your word.
    2. It builds your first store in the foreground, with a live progress line,
      3. and prints the moment you can start asking. Right after, still in the foreground, it renders the AI agent sessions on this disk (Claude Code, Codex) into the chats scope - the same step the hourly pass runs, so they answer now and not an hour later - and says how many it rendered. Once, it also says what this disk cannot hold: sessions run on your other devices and the providers' hosted chats come in through a data export you request from the provider, fed to docenta ingest claude-ai <manifest> (claude.ai) or docenta ingest chatgpt <download> (ChatGPT). The ledger's chats row records the count.
    3. It starts the semantic layers in the background.
    4. It registers the hourly refresh with your system's scheduler, for the
      5. store it is onboarding: the machine's store under the label every install carries, a named store or another data dir under a job of its own (section 7.2). The schedule : line names the store the job serves.
    5. It runs the hand-offs you asked for: the agents, then the mail account.

    Every answer lands in the capability ledger, which docenta setup answers prints: the semantic rows follow the word you gave (turbo and local are on, lazy is lazy, later is deferred), OCR and the archives say what you answered, and mail and agents say whether the hand-off connected anything or what to run later. A scope without an archive has no mailbox row at all.

    Tip

    You can stop it at any point with Ctrl-C. Run the same command again and it carries on with what is still missing; it never repeats work that is done. The answers you had given, on the page or in the terminal, are kept in a draft: the next run says "An onboarding was interrupted N min ago with K answers" and asks once whether to continue with them (the pace included, never asked again) or start fresh; --fresh starts fresh without asking, and a draft for another scope is discarded on its own. docenta setup onboard --reset is a different thing: it starts the store over, shows what it would delete, asks, and then begins fresh.

    On macOS the system asks, folder by folder, whether docenta may read. Answer once for each, or give your terminal Full Disk Access (System Settings, Privacy and Security) and the questions go away for good. Windows and Linux ask nothing.

    Useful flags: --step (always confirm each phase), --cli-only (every decision in the terminal, no page in the browser), --fresh (discard an interrupted run's answers), --reset (start the store over). A script answers the questions without a terminal: --yes takes every default, --embed local|turbo|lazy|later gives the word, and --ocr on|later, --mail now|later, --agents now|later, --mbox now|later answer the four questions above. --yes asks nothing at all: the agents found are connected without the per-client question, and the mail question stands on later with the one line to run (docenta setup mail), because the key is typed at a keyboard.

    3.3 The runtime and the models#

    docenta runs its AI models on your own machine, through the ONNX Runtime. Onboarding fetches both for you. Everything comes from dl.docenta.ai and from nowhere else, and every file is checked against a signed index before it is used. Nothing is downloaded while you search, and no model ever sends anything anywhere.

    ModelIts job
    arctic-embed-m-v2.0The embedder: turns a passage into the numbers that make search by meaning work.
    sparse-doc-v3-distillThe sparse encoder: adds related words to each passage. The single strongest ranking signal.
    bge-reranker-baseThe reranker: a last careful reader that puts the best few answers in order.
    arctic-embed-m-v2.0-fixed32x512Apple Silicon only: the same embedder with its inputs fixed at 32 passages of 512 tokens, the form Apple's GPU can run. Identical vectors, about twice the CPU's speed.
    sparse-doc-v3-distill-fixed32x512Apple Silicon only: the sparse encoder in the same fixed form, for the GPU. The same terms, about twice the CPU's speed on an M4 Max and more on a slower CPU.
    bge-reranker-base-fixed16x512Apple Silicon only: the re-ranker with its inputs fixed at 16 question-passage pairs of 512 tokens, for the GPU. The same ranking, a search page re-ranked in about a third of the CPU's time (162 against 560 ms on an M4 Max). The first search after install compiles it once, about a minute.

    On a Mac with Apple Silicon the embedder runs on the GPU. Apple's GPU cannot execute the model as it ships (its input sizes vary), so the assets carry a fixed-size copy of the same weights and docenta-setup installs it on Apple Silicon only. The first embed run compiles it for your chip and macOS, which takes one to two minutes and is kept (in the variant's coreml-cache folder); every later run starts from that. Before its first vector counts, the lane is checked against the CPU on probe texts, and a machine without the variant, or where the check fails, embeds on the CPU and says why in its armed line. Measured on an M4 Max: 57 passages a second on the GPU against 25 on all sixteen CPU cores, with the CPU left free. The sparse encoder does the same with its own variant (3,131 passages a minute against 1,760), checked term by term against the CPU before it counts. DOCENTA_EMBED_ACCEL=cpu and DOCENTA_SPARSE_ACCEL=cpu keep either on the CPU.

    To check what is installed, without changing anything:

    bash
    docenta setup verify

    It prints one line per item, for example runtime : onnxruntime 1.28.0 present and model : arctic-embed-m-v2.0 ... present. To fetch anything that is missing, run docenta setup update (section 3.5): it is safe to run at any time and downloads only what is absent or behind.

    Where they land:

    macOS   ~/Library/Application Support/docenta/
Linux   ~/.local/share/docenta/
Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\docenta\data\

    with the runtime under onnxruntime and the models under models. docenta setup config prints the exact places on your machine. If you keep the runtime somewhere else, set ORT_DYLIB_PATH to the full path of the library file and every binary uses it.

    Note

    If the models are missing, docenta still works: keyword search, reading the evidence and the MCP tools need no model at all. Only the meaning layer waits for them.

    3.4 Verify the installation#

    bash
    docenta --version
docenta setup config

    docenta setup config prints every location docenta uses and what decided it. Before onboarding has run, most rows say (absent); that is expected.

    3.5 Staying current#

    bash
    docenta setup update

    That one command is the whole upkeep (docenta setup update starts the installer program of this install, docenta-setup). It follows the channel this machine was installed from (the installer records it; --channel family picks another one and records that). In order, it:

    1. holds the hourly sync for the swap when a new build is due (it writes
      2. the pause marker ~/.docenta/sync.pause and lifts it at the end; a pause you set yourself with docenta schedule pause is left exactly as it was; a sync pass already running finishes, because the swap is atomic);
    2. fetches the newest build, verifies its signature and digest, and swaps
      3. every binary in place;
    3. brings the models and the ONNX runtime current: every model and
      4. accelerator variant this platform installs, the ones published since your install included, each verified the same way the install was;
    4. checks the result: every installed binary runs and names the channel's
      5. build, every model is present and current, and the installed runtime carries the platform's lane (cpu, coreml on Apple Silicon, cpu, directml on Windows - never a quiet fallback to the CPU, section 9.5);
    5. migrates the scheduled jobs: every docenta job this machine's
      6. scheduler holds (launchd, Task Scheduler, systemd) whose command still spells the pass verb an older build wrote is rewritten by the NEW binary to update --scheduled and reloaded, with its store flags, its interval or time of day, its log paths and its priority exactly as they were (docenta schedule migrate is the same step by hand; --dry-run shows what it would rewrite). A job that is not docenta's is never read; a job already current is counted as such;
    6. refreshes the agent configs docenta already manages (Claude Code, Codex,
      7. Cursor), the same merge docenta agents add makes, each written file read back and checked. A client docenta was never set up in is left alone; adding one stays docenta agents add;
    7. starts the timed pass: for every store whose job it migrated or whose
      8. binary it swapped, ONE docenta update --scheduled --after-swap runs detached (its console goes to the store's sync.log). It waits for the setup's own hold to lift (a pause you set yourself stands, and the pass stands down), then for a pass already running on the store (the reloaded job runs at load), each wait bounded at fifteen minutes; then it runs the whole pass, records its wall time as every whole update does and, because it runs outside the job, re-registers the job with the cadence it earns (section 7.2: under thirty minutes earns hourly, longer the nightly setting). A store with a pass running when the setup looks is skipped with a line: that pass's own time is the measurement, and the next by-hand docenta update applies it. The setup does not wait for the pass; docenta schedule status shows the result when it ends (measured: last pass 12 s).

    It prints a short summary and one verdict:

    build       : docenta 0.3.1 (aaaaaaa1) -> v0.3.2+bbbbbbb (family)
changed     : 6 binaries, 1 model
checked     : every binary runs v0.3.2+bbbbbbb, all 7 models current, lane coreml carried
jobs        : 1 rewritten to `update --scheduled` (net.docenta.sync), 1 current
agents      : claude-code, codex refreshed
measuring   : a timed pass runs detached for the machine's store (pid 4242); the schedule follows it (docenta schedule status shows the result)
ready       : yes

    When something fails, the last line is ready : no - followed by what failed and what to do, and the command exits non-zero. -v (or --verbose) prints every step and check as it happens. A running docenta swaps to the new build by itself; chapter 9 has the details.

    docenta setup verify is the read-only check: the channel's signature and digest, every binary in its build runs and names it, every model present and current here, the runtime's lane carried. It installs nothing and ends with the same verdict line.

    3.6 Taking it off again#

    Two commands, because they undo two different things. docenta uninstall walks back what onboarding built on this machine, part by part, after telling you what your first build cost. docenta uninstall binaries takes the programs themselves, the inverse of the install line. Your own files are never a part of either. Chapter 8 describes both.

    4. First run: from zero to your first answer#

    4.1 Ask what it will cost (optional but recommended)#

    bash
    docenta setup estimate --preset repo

    profile    : Full (16 cores, 64 GiB RAM, 55 GiB free, hash 1724 MiB/s)
scope      : /Users/you/code/project - 25000 files, 10 GiB (sample capped; scale estimates up)
lexical T1 : est 1 min (searchable with receipts as it streams)
semantic T2: est 25 min background

    It measures your machine, classifies it (Full, Standard, Constrained, or Refuse if there is not enough disk to work safely), counts the scope by the ingest's own exclusion policy (the directories the ingest will enter and no others - the hygiene globs, the marker-qualified names, the crumbs, the gitignore chains and the store's own data; the counted row says "by the ingest policy"), reads a sample of its files through the real extraction lanes, and estimates every step. The semantic steps (sparse terms, dense chunks) are sized the way the pipeline itself counts them: a uniform draw of the scope's files is read and its units counted by the index step's own rules, the scope's largest files are read outright rather than inferred, and the rest is projected per byte and per extension - a file's units follow its text, not its being a file, so a sample's few large files never stand for every small one. Files larger than the sample reads (16 MiB) are not projected at all: a mail archive or a database dump the sample never opened is named on the screen as unmeasured rather than guessed from a neighbour's rate. The units row on the screen says what it rests on: the sample's size, how much of its text sat in its largest files, what lies beyond the sample's reach, and whether a ceiling decided (a scope cannot hold more chunks of 200 characters than its text-bearing bytes allow; when the sample's rate says more, the ceiling is quoted and the row says CAPPED). The rate lines name their lane (on cpu, on coreml): on an Intel Mac both model lanes run on the cpu, and a rate in the low hundreds a minute is that machine, not a bad day. Presets are repo (the git repository you are standing in), essentials (~/Documents), and machine (every fixed volume: / on macOS and Linux, each drive letter on Windows; everything says the same). docenta setup onboard without --root takes the machine, so the first build and the hourly refresh walk the same roots and the sizing quotes what the refresh will bring; the root row then reads / (the whole machine) or lists the volumes. --root DIR names any folder, and the hourly refresh then keeps to that folder. The operating system's own trees (/usr, /opt, /System, the system /Library, C:\Windows, C:\Program Files and their kin, section 5.8 rule 2) are not part of a machine scope; your home, every mounted drive and every other drive root are.

    4.2 Create the store#

    bash
    docenta store init

    One time, idempotent. It creates the data directory layout and the state database. Safe to re-run - it is also how schema migrations get applied after an upgrade.

    4.3 Your first ingest - start small#

    Tip

    Do not point it at your whole machine yet. Pick one folder you know well, so the first answers come from files you can judge:

    bash
    docenta ingest folder ~/Documents -v

    -v shows progress. What happens: docenta walks the folder, identifies each file's family, hashes its content, extracts text from the formats it knows, and indexes it. Re-running costs almost nothing because unchanged files are skipped by content.

    Useful flags: --family document (only PDFs, Office files, mail), --ext pdf,eml, --full (ignore the change journal and re-walk everything), --json (machine-readable output).

    4.4 Your first search#

    You can search while the ingest is still running:

    bash
    docenta search "something you know is in there"
docenta status --content

    If you get hits, the engine half is working. This is the point where docenta is already useful.

    4.5 Build the meaning layer#

    bash
    docenta layers pipeline -v

    (docenta layers ... starts the meaning layer's program, docenta-semantic, from this install.) This runs eight steps in dependency order, each resuming from its own cursor:

    StepWhat it builds
    1. indexthe unit-level keyword index (finer-grained than file level)
    2. embeddense vectors with the production embedder
    3. embed (code)vectors for code symbols, if the code model is installed
    4. mentionsevery mention of a person, company, address, or account
    5. entitiesresolves those mentions into entities
    6. gazetteerbinds aliases and spelling variants
    7. claimsbuilds the claims graph that timelines read
    8. communitiesdetects themes running across everything you indexed
    Note

    The first run over a large collection takes hours; you can stop it at any time with Ctrl-C and re-run later. Steps that need a missing model skip with a message rather than failing - if you never installed the code embedder, step 3 prints no code model installed - skipped and the pipeline continues.

    Watch it from another terminal:

    bash
    docenta layers status --watch

    4.6 Now go wide#

    Once the small scope worked end to end, index the machine:

    bash
    docenta ingest machine          # every fixed drive, into one shared collection
docenta ingest machine --plan   # dry run: show what it would do first

    ingest machine gives each root its own incremental cursor, so later runs only look at what changed - on macOS it uses FSEvents, on Windows the NTFS change journal. The cursor reads a folder renamed out of the scope as the departure of everything under it (the journal names the folder and none of its files), so those rows are held as missing at the next update, the way a file's own delete holds its row; a folder renamed in is walked. Every path the cursor reports is spelled under the root as you gave it, even where the filesystem resolves the root elsewhere (/tmp to /private/tmp on macOS). A change record the Windows journal cannot place - its parent folder no longer resolves by id - is not dropped: it is a resolve row of docenta status --waiting, and the recover step returns to it by what the record says.

    4.7 Connect your agent#

    bash
    claude mcp add --scope user docenta -- ~/.docenta/bin/docenta serve

    Then ask your agent something only your files would know. See chapter 5.7 for other clients and the full tool list.

    5. Using docenta day to day#

    There are two ways to use docenta: the command line (you type, you read) and an AI agent over MCP (your agent searches on your behalf). They serve the same data. Start with the command line so you can see what the agent sees.

    5.1 Keyword search: docenta search#

    The workhorse. Fast, literal, and available the moment your first ingest starts, with no models involved.

    bash
    docenta search "water heater invoice"

    The page, from a folder of three notes:

    has_more: false
next_offset: 2
strict_hits: 2
total_hits: 2

results:
  1. ~/house/water-heater.md  2026-11-13
  # Water heater The tankless water heater was installed in March 2016. The installer left the invo...
  family text  provenance first_party  raw_score 12.126  score 12.126  size_bytes 230
  content_id blake3:4aab14073d762c9b7b22d2483ca8fcd38c2628d4af069121a8472f1dca254fd8
  2. ~/house/invoice-2016-031.txt  2026-11-13
  Invoice 2016-031 Water heater, tankless, installed Total 1,480.00
  family text  provenance first_party  raw_score 6.395  score 6.395  size_bytes 66
  content_id blake3:4ed9ba5eb9397def66914fb4c5e44b4ab8acd08a39cb48175292d2fdbdeb94da
answered_from: lexical
related_terms: installed; tankless

more under --json: retrieval_path

    search is the tool your agent calls under the same name, typed: the flags are the tool's parameters, --json prints the reply the agent gets, and the page above is that reply laid out for reading. Read it like this:

    • The top lines are what the reply says about itself. A notice: line,
      • when there is one, comes first and is the line to read first: it says when the page is not what you typed (a word dropped, a broader search). strict_hits is how many documents held every word; has_more and next_offset are the next page.
    • Each result is headed by where the file lives now and its date.
    • The second line is real text from the document, not a summary, cut to
      • one line (--json carries it whole, with snippet_offset_chars).
    • The third line is what else the hit says about itself. score only
      • orders the page; its absolute value means nothing. A flag that is off and a count of nothing are not printed, so what you see is what is so:
    • archived true - this copy was found only in a backup or export, so the
      • values in it may be out of date.
    • external true - vendored or system material (toolchains, dependency
      • trees), ranked slightly lower on purpose.
    • conversation true - an AI chat transcript; claims in it date from when
      • the conversation happened.
    • duplicates N / near_duplicates N - identical or near-identical
      • copies were folded into this one row.
    • content_id blake3:... identifies the *content*, not the path, and it
      • is what you pass to read to read more.

    With --json every hit that can say so also carries source_role: what kind of source it is (governing, historical_record, derived_session, external_reference) and whether your store's [[serve.authority]] table declared it or its path only suggests it (inferred). No role means unknown, not "current". A page whose every hit is an agent session or a system or vendored file says so in its notice: your own note may hold all but one of the words.

    Useful flags:

    FlagWhat it does
    --mode phraseMatch words next to each other, like "main drain test".
    --mode regexMatch a regular expression against body tokens.
    --families documentOnly search PDFs, Office files, email. Repeatable, or a comma list.
    --extensions pdf,emlOnly these file extensions.
    --scopes mailOnly these scopes: mail, chats, git, repo:<name>, origin:<name>.
    --modified-after 2026-01-01 / --date-before 2026-03-01A date window (a mail's Date, a file's modification time otherwise).
    --latestNewest first.
    --limit 25More hits per page (the server caps at 50).
    --offset NNext page: pass the next_offset the previous page printed; it is a cursor into the index, not a count of hits shown (a long document is several index rows, so the offset can pass the total while more is available). Paging reaches every distinct match; a row can occasionally come back on a later page (its content id tells), and refining the query is usually faster than paging deep.
    --response-format conciseThe stored document head as the snippet (a listing). The default snippet is a real match window from the body, with snippet_offset_chars for the read.
    --no-fold-near-duplicatesShow every near-identical copy as its own row. Every switch has such an opposite (--no-latest, --no-exclude-own-session).
    --jsonThe reply as your agent gets it.
    --directAnswer in this process even when the store's server is running (the default asks the running server, which is already warm).
    --exclude-own-sessionLeave out the calling agent's own session transcript and every copy of it (the session named by DOCENTA_AGENT_SESSION, Codex's CODEX_THREAD_ID or Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID; two that disagree exclude nothing, and the page says so); off by default, so past sessions stay searchable. Over MCP, Codex names the calling thread in every tool call, so each Codex thread leaves out only its own transcript even when many share one server.

    The habit that works: run several cheap, narrow searches instead of one broad search and deep paging. Docenta is built for iteration - a query costs milliseconds.

    Identifiers stay whole. When no document holds every word, docenta drops words one at a time until a combination holds. A word joined by -, _ or . (live-overlaid, AAPL_100) counts as one word in that climb when it occurs whole somewhere, so it is never cut in half; only a joined word that appears nowhere whole has its parts searched apart. The NOTICE: line says which (kept live-overlaid whole).

    When a search comes back empty or weak, read coverage before rewording. The page then says what the store knows about capture, from receipts only, and the first finding opens the NOTICE: line: a capture step that failed on its last run, a date window that starts after the last successful capture (the mail is not captured yet), captured documents still waiting for the index, a scope the store holds nothing of, and on a mail question the accounts the store holds (mail of any other account is simply not here). --json carries it all under freshness, with each asked scope's newest document date (the document's own date, not when it was ingested), its last ingest stamp and its capture step's last success, null when no receipt exists. No receipt means "unknown", never "behind". A sealed collection speaks only of its seal. Nothing here starts a pass; docenta update --scheduled (or the agent's refresh) does.

    5.2 Reading the evidence: docenta read#

    Search tells you *where*; read shows you *what*. Pass the content id from a hit, or the file's path:

    bash
    docenta read blake3:4aab14073d762c9b7b22d2483ca8fcd38c2628d4af069121a8472f1dca254fd8 \
  --around-match "invoice" --max-chars 120

     heater was installed in March 2016.
The installer left the invoice in the kitchen drawer: 1,480 dollars, paid by check.
-- chars 34..154 of 230; next: --offset-chars 154
-- canonical_path: ~/house/water-heater.md
-- content_id: blake3:4aab14073d762c9b7b22d2483ca8fcd38c2628d4af069121a8472f1dca254fd8
-- match_found: true
-- date: 2026-11-13
-- title: Water heater

    The text comes first, as it is; every line that begins -- is what the reply says about it: where the window sits in the document and how to continue, which file it is, whether the words asked for were found. --around-match TEXT centers the window on the first occurrence of that text, which is almost always what you want. read is the tool your agent calls under the same name, so the other flags are the tool's parameters:

    FlagDefaultWhat it does
    --max-chars N8000Size of the window (200,000 at most).
    --offset-chars N0Where the window starts: pass the next: offset to continue.
    --structure / --structure localoffThe document's captured structure beside the text (its tables, sheets, notes, a code file's declarations), whole in pages or this window's neighbourhood only; --json carries it.
    --representation KEY-Read one body of the content when the same bytes were read under two recipes (a hit names its representation).
    --jsonoffThe reply as your agent gets it.
    --directoffAnswer in this process even when the store's server is running.

    What sits beside a document (a message's attachments, a folder's neighbours) is docenta related, and the conversation a message belongs to is docenta thread; both take the same id or path.

    docenta serves the text it extracted, and never a copy of your file: the original stays where it is, and that is where you open it.

    5.3 What is in there: status --content, dev families, status --waiting#

    bash
    docenta status --content

    content objects : 842434
file instances  : 2878922
by family       : text 331705, document 280326, image 223269, animated 1576, media 5534, archive 24
last ingest     : 1786485814175 (unix ms)

    Content objects are distinct pieces of content; file instances are paths pointing at them. The gap between those two numbers is your duplication (here: 2.88 million paths hold 842 thousand distinct contents).

    • docenta status --storage - how much disk each store uses.
    • docenta status --by-drive - per-drive breakdown.
    • docenta dev families - the modality ladder, with which extensions belong to
      • each family.
    • docenta status --waiting image - files identified as a family but not yet
      • processed by their lane: the "pre-approved queue". Each row carries the reason it waits (no lane reads .dylib; a binary format no lane reads, over the sniff size limit (limits.sniff_max_bytes); ...), and --waiting unknown lists the files of no family at all.
    • docenta setup config - every path docenta uses and *what decided it*. This is
      • the always-correct answer to "where does everything live".

    5.4 Semantic search: meaning, not spelling#

    Once chapter 4's pipeline has run, the second binary answers questions where you do not know the words used in the document.

    bash
    docenta dev probe search "how do we compress sidecars"   # keyword over units
docenta dev probe dense "how do we compress sidecars"    # meaning only
docenta dev probe hybrid "how do we compress sidecars"   # all channels fused

    (docenta dev probe ... is the same command; the probes are an instrument and docenta layers --help does not list them.)

    Use hybrid by default. It runs the keyword, meaning, and learned-sparse channels together and fuses them by rank agreement - when independent methods agree on a document, that agreement is the strongest signal available. Its output shows exactly which channels voted:

    [ 415583] lex#4+dense#4+sparse#1 content=d4c65f12a80e (+2 same content)
[ 266483] dense#18+sparse#3 content=877554acf5aa

    Read that as: the top hit was ranked 4th by keyword, 4th by meaning, and 1st by the sparse channel. A hit that only one channel found is worth more skepticism than one all three found. Agreement says where to read first, not that the document answers the question: two channels can agree on a passage from the wrong year. Over MCP, search_meaning reports this as admission.verdict: empty (nothing was served, no evidence either way), channels_agree, single_channel (read each hit on its merits) or unassessed (a layer is still building).

    Common flags: --limit N (default 10), --json, and --rerank to enable the cross-encoder re-ranking stage (off by default: it was measured to cost most of the query budget without improving answers on this material).

    5.5 The evidence pack: one assembled briefing#

    The flagship read surface. Instead of a list of links, it assembles one answer-shaped object: the route it chose, the cited evidence, connections between items, conflicts it found, and - importantly - an explicit list of what it could not see.

    bash
    docenta ask "what did we decide about the firewall design" --token-budget 2000

    (docenta ask is the evidence tool an agent calls, typed: the same parameters as flags, the same reply under --json.)

    route      : fallback (no structural signal)
budget     : 782/800 tokens [trimmed]
  blake3:d0de68d4...  1786240805  <subject line>
   > <a short excerpt of the passage, word for word>
     /path/to/the/source @1840 unit 6f2a...
  blake3:91c0e2aa...  1786100114  <subject line>
  ...
  ! no structural route: evidence is lexical/hybrid ranked
  ! budget trimmed evidence: 10 of 20 units shown, 0 excerpts left out

    Up to four of the cited units carry an excerpt: a short passage copied word for word from the document, the place in the document where the question's distinctive words meet. The line below it is the locator: the source's path, the character offset the excerpt starts at, and the passage's unit id, so docenta read <id> --offset-chars <offset> (or the MCP read tool with that unit_id) opens exactly that place. The excerpt slots go first to one passage for each distinctive word of the question, then to one for each kind of source the pack cites (commits, sessions, a repository's files, mail), so two documents that each answer half of a question both show their half; a passage repeated word for word takes no second slot, but its document stays cited. The other units are listed by id, date and subject.

    The lines starting with ! are the honest part: the pack tells you when its route was a guess and when the token budget forced it to leave evidence out. --token-budget N (default 2000) sets the token ceiling for the whole pack, excerpts included; the pack enforces it rather than overflowing your agent's context, and when it must cut, the units without an excerpt go first.

    --scopes SCOPE (repeatable: repo:<name>, git, chats, mail, origin:<name>, the spellings search takes) draws the evidence from those worlds only. Without it the pack applies a scope the question names itself (a repo: token, a repository named in a question about code, a path like crates/x/src/lib.rs) and says so; if that scope holds nothing, it searches everything and says that too. The pack also says what its evidence can and cannot carry, about the passages it cited and nothing more:

      ! 4 citations hold none of the question's distinctive words (...); they are listed last
  ! never seen in repo:docenta, git, chats: kafka
  ! assessment: lexical check: none of the 12 examined passages holds more than 1 of ... together. That is no evidence either way: they may answer in other words or another language, so read them; ...
  ! limit: the budget trimmed the pack: more evidence was found than is cited
  ! limit: no excerpt holds kafka: read the cited documents; the answer may use other words or lie in a document the pack does not cite
  ! dates: the question asks about in 2023; the 9 dated passages examined carry document dates from 2025 to 2026 ...

    The assessment is a word check, not a judgement of truth. When the question's distinctive words meet in one cited passage it says to read that passage first, which is not proof that it answers: a note that discusses a migration you decided against holds every word of "when did we migrate". When they do not meet, that is no evidence either way: a passage in other words or another language holds an answer as readily as one that holds none, so read the passages, then try search_meaning. The pack does not say whether your documents hold an answer; the passages do. A limit: line names what the check could not see (a trimmed budget, documents not indexed yet or not yours to read), and a dates: line appears when the question names a year that every dated passage lies outside; those dates are the documents' own, not the dates of the events they describe. In JSON and over MCP the same is the pack's assessment object (anchors: anchors_cooccur, anchors_partial, anchors_absent or not_assessed).

    A route that found an entity or a time window joins the keyword evidence instead of replacing it. The MCP evidence tool takes the same scopes.

    5.6 People, timelines, and themes#

    These layers are built by the pipeline in chapter 4 and answer the questions that plain search cannot.

    bash
    docenta layers graph entities --card "Acme Plumbing"     # everything about one entity
docenta layers graph claims --timeline "Acme Plumbing"   # what happened, when, with evidence
docenta layers graph communities --list                  # themes running through it all
docenta layers graph modules --list                      # code modules, if you index code

    (docenta starts docenta-semantic graph ... for it.)

    The entity layer is deterministic: every link traces back to the exact mentions that produced it, and you can overrule it. --accept and --reject record a human verdict that the machine will not undo.

    5.7 Giving it to your AI agent (MCP)#

    This is what docenta is really for. The server runs over stdio and is started by your MCP client, not by you.

    Claude Code (one command, from anywhere):

    bash
    claude mcp add docenta ~/.docenta/bin/docenta serve

    Claude Desktop or any other MCP client - add this to the client's config file (on macOS, ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json):

    json
    {
  "mcpServers": {
 "docenta": {
   "type": "stdio",
   "command": "/Users/YOU/.docenta/bin/docenta",
   "args": ["serve"],
   "env": {}
 }
  }
}
    Warning

    Use the full absolute path to the binary; MCP clients do not always inherit your shell's PATH.

    Once connected, your agent has twenty-one tools:

    ToolWhat the agent uses it forNeeds
    helpThe built-in workflows, and the guide, examples or contract of one toolnothing
    searchKeyword, phrase, or regex search with family/extension/date/mail filtersnothing
    readRead a window of one document, centered on the matchnothing
    locateWhere something lives, by meaning, without the passage textmodels + pipeline
    statusCorpus size, families, freshness per scope, and build status so it can narrate the waitnothing
    doctorOne verdict page for the box: PATH, build, models, layers, sync, turbo, mail, each with its fix; --fix runs the quick onesnothing (--fix runs the fixes it names)
    check_pathIs this exact path stored, and under which content idnothing
    relatedWhat sits beside or above a hit: the carrying message, folder siblingsnothing
    threadA mail conversation in order, from any one of its messagesnothing
    refreshA freshness pass now (chats, mail, scan); fire-and-forgetnothing (writes)
    operation_statusHow a refresh or a build is doing, read-onlynothing
    focusTell the background embedder which path the current work is about, so its content comes firstnothing (writes)
    licenseThe lease this box runs on and what it allowsnothing
    search_meaningMeaning-based search over the fused channels; each answer shows and names the passage that matched (where your words occur together when they do, else the part of a long document that matched by meaning), which read opens; also_matched names the other place when there were twomodels + pipeline
    evidenceOne assembled, budgeted briefing with gaps declaredmodels + pipeline
    verify_quoteVerify a quote actually appears in a document before repeating itnothing
    save_noteKeep a note in the corpus for the next sessionnothing (writes)
    who_isEverything about a person, company, or projectentity store
    correct_personMerge or split a person the entity store got wrongentity store (writes)
    timelineWhat happened in a given year, with evidenceentity store
    themesDetected communities and themes across everything indexedentity store
    surveyOne screen about a question before reading: the sources by scope and count, the families, the date span, the threads and folders with the most hits, the people the index matches, each line with the id that expands it; expand leads with read on a sample id; channel: meaning folds the meaning page insteadnothing (people need the entity store; the meaning channel needs the semantic layers)

    The four tools marked "writes" change the store or the session. A store several people or agents share can be served without them: docenta serve --read-only, or read_only = true under [serve] in the config, lists only the other seventeen and refuses the four by name. A read-only session shares the store's hub with every other session (since 2026-11-09; before that it ran a brain of its own, and on a Mac Studio four read-only clients each opened the store for themselves, 45 to 75 s and 868 MB a piece while a pass ran): the shared brain serves every tool, and the session's own docenta serve keeps the writing tools out of its tool list and refuses them by name.

    Two things worth knowing:

    • The tools are always registered, even before the models are installed.
      • If a tool needs a layer you have not built yet, it says so in plain words and names the command that builds it, rather than disappearing.
    • The server re-checks on every call, so a layer you build while the
      • agent is running mounts by itself. No restart needed.
    • Every result fits one tool call. A search, search_meaning,
      • locate or evidence reply is bounded to 32 KiB of JSON by default (a detailed 50-hit search measured up to 130 KB before): the server keeps concise rows - which document, where in it, what caveats - and as much detail as fits, and its reply_budget says what it cut and the exact read call that brings it back. A reply that fits is unchanged. The 32 KiB is docenta's default, chosen from measured replies and client behaviour, not a limit of the MCP protocol.
    • docenta serve is self-upgrading: when you install a new binary, the
      • store's hub hands over to one of the new build (it leaves as soon as no call is in flight, and every connected session re-attaches on its next line), so neither the next session nor the running ones need a config change. Until 2026-11-09 the hub swapped only its brain and stayed on as the old build; a hub running from the file the update had deleted could not be trusted by any new session, and held the lock against a fresh one for as long as its sessions kept it alive. A hub of such an earlier build is recognised by the first session of the new build (your process, a deleted file or the update's aside, serve --hub for this store) and ended, and a hub of the new build starts in its place.
    • The handshake is answered at once, before the store is open. A
      • cold start (no hub running yet) opens the store and loads the semantic engine, which on a large store takes well over ten seconds, and Codex gives a server ten seconds to answer initialize before it gives up on it ("timed out handshaking with MCP server after 9.999999959s", field 2026-10-09). So docenta serve answers initialize and the tool list right away, from what this store's brain said on its last start (or this build's own roster the first time), and reaches the hub behind it; the first tool call waits for the store to open and is answered then, or, past 20 seconds, with "docenta is still starting (the store is opening, N s so far); retry" rather than hanging (20, since 2026-11-09: below the shortest client clock we know of, Claude Code's 30 s; the earlier 45 s answered exactly when a 45 s client gave up). If the brain that comes up is another build than the one the handshake named, the session is asked to list its tools again.
    • A connected session is asked to re-list its tools when a new build
      • serves: the server declares tools.listChanged and sends notifications/tools/list_changed - from the hub to every session attached at the swap, and from the session's own shim when the binary changes while the hub has dropped the session for a day's silence, or when a reconnect lands on another build. An agent client that honours the notification picks up renamed or new tools by itself; one that does not keeps its connect-time roster until it reconnects. If an agent's toolset and its instructions disagree about the names, one status call settles it: tool_names is the date of the name generation the serving build uses (2026-09-22 for search, read, who_is, ...), and a roster that still shows content_search is the client's cache - tell it to reconnect.
    • Upgrade with docenta setup update and with nothing else. It replaces
      • each binary temp-then-rename, which is ATOMIC: an observer sees the whole old file or the whole new one. Never rm the binary and then cp a new one over the gap - a 31 MB copy leaves seconds where the file on disk is half-written, and anything that inspects it then (the supervisor included) sees a binary that cannot run. Measured 2026-08-18: that non-atomic pattern is what dropped two connected agent sessions during a run of rapid redeploys.

    5.7.1 From another machine: ssh and stdio#

    Docenta serves MCP over stdio and its hub listens on local IPC only, by design: there is no HTTP transport and no port to open. An agent on another machine (a Linux box, a laptop) reaches the store the same way the agents on the store's machine do, with ssh carrying the stdio. The store, the models and the sync stay on the one machine that holds the files; the other machine needs ssh and nothing of docenta.

    Field 2026-11-09 (a Mac Studio holding the store, an Ubuntu box running Codex and an agent framework over Tailscale): this is what worked, and what to set.

    1. A key and a host alias. Key-based ssh from the client to the
      2. store's machine, BatchMode=yes so a missing key fails at once instead of asking, and a host alias (mac-studio below) in ~/.ssh/config on the client so the server line stays short.
    1. The server line. The client starts docenta serve on the
      2. store's machine through ssh. Codex (~/.codex/config.toml on the client):
    toml
    [mcp_servers.docenta]
command = "ssh"
args = ["-o", "BatchMode=yes", "-o", "ServerAliveInterval=30",
        "mac-studio", "/Users/USER/.docenta/bin/docenta", "serve", "--read-only"]
startup_timeout_sec = 60
tool_timeout_sec = 300

    Claude Code, from the client:

    bash
    claude mcp add docenta -- ssh -o BatchMode=yes mac-studio /Users/USER/.docenta/bin/docenta serve --read-only

    Use the binary's full path on the store's machine: a non-interactive ssh session does not read the login shell's PATH.

    1. --read-only for a client that should not write. The remote
      2. session then lists and answers the reading tools only (save_note, refresh, focus and correct_person are neither listed nor callable) and still shares the store's warm hub with the sessions on the machine itself. Leave the flag off for a client you trust to write notes.
    1. The first call after a quiet spell waits. The handshake is
      2. answered at once, but when no hub is running the first tool call waits for the store to open (well over ten seconds on a large store, longer while a pass runs) and past 20 seconds is answered with "the store is opening, N s so far; retry". Give the client a tool timeout of a minute or more (Codex's tool_timeout_sec above), and let the agent retry a busy answer. The hub stays up for ten minutes after the last session leaves (DOCENTA_HUB_IDLE_SECS), so a client that returns within that window finds the store open.
    1. One hub, many clients. Every session over ssh, from any machine,
      2. attaches to the same hub as the local ones; docenta serve --status on the store's machine lists them under clients. Nothing listens on an IP address, before or after.
    1. Measuring a slow open. When the first call waits long, the brain
      2. says where the time went. Call status with detail: true (the compact page carries neither server nor semantic_mount) and read server.store_open: total_ms and phases, a list with one {phase, ms} per phase of the open, in the order they ran (layout_and_state, lexical_index, identities, principal, structure_source, sync_layout, corpus_card); semantic_mount on the same page times the dense layers, which mount behind the open on their own thread. The same numbers are in the quiet log on the store's machine, <data root>/logs/docenta.log (by default ~/.docenta/logs/docenta.log), as one line per brain start: store open: N ms in all (...), beside the hub's line hub: the brain (generation G) answered initialize after N ms and listed its tools after M ms. Take one reading while a sync pass runs and one while none does; the difference is the pass's share. scripts/field/measure-store-open.sh (in the repository) takes both readings unattended with a brain of its own (DOCENTA_SERVE_MODE=direct, so nothing has to be stopped) and writes one log file to send; with --update it runs docenta setup update first, with --upload URL it sends the file itself when it is done (a presigned address the receiver minted), and on a Mac it keeps the machine awake for the run. Whoever asks for the readings can bake both into the copy they send, so the person holding the store types one command and leaves.

    What this does not give you: a connector that needs an HTTP endpoint (ChatGPT's remote connectors, for one) has nothing to connect to; a proxy of your own in front of ssh is the only way there, and it is yours to secure.

    5.7.1 From a script, or an agent that works through a shell#

    Everything an agent can ask over MCP can be typed. Each tool is a verb with the tool's own parameters as flags, and --json prints the reply the agent would get:

    bash
    docenta meaning "who agreed to the roof repair" --scopes mail --limit 5 --json
docenta ask "what did we decide about the firewall" --token-budget 2000 --json
docenta who "Thomas" --json
docenta verify "the roof repair was agreed in March" ~/notes/roof.md --json

    When the store's hub is running (an agent session is open), a typed verb is answered by it, so docenta meaning pays the answer and not the model load; otherwise it answers in its own process (--direct forces that).

    docenta help --json prints every command with its arguments and flags, and the exit codes:

    exitcodemeaning
    0donethe command did what it was asked
    1failedthe command ran and failed
    2usagethe command line was wrong; nothing ran
    3not_foundwhat was asked for is not in the store
    4not_permittedthe seal, a hold, the license or a read-only store refuses it
    5busyanother docenta run holds the store; the same command later works
    75try_laternot now: something is still starting or not built yet; retryable says whether the same command is enough

    With --json, a failure is one object on standard error:

    json
    {"error":{"code":"sealed","exit":4,"retryable":false,
 "fix":"docenta store unseal","message":"the store is sealed: ..."}}

    --no-input makes sure nothing waits for a person: a command that would ask a question fails with exit 2 and names the flag that answers it.

    A long run (an update, an ingest, the layers' pipeline, a cloud ship) says what it is doing while it runs: under --json every step is one JSON object per line on standard error, and standard output stays the one object at the end.

    json
    {"progress":{"message":"step started","step":"scan","at_unix":1794634440}}
{"progress":{"message":"step ended","step_done":"scan","secs":3,"failed":false,"at_unix":1794634443}}

    A command that is done within a second prints none of these lines. An error object is told apart by its key, error.

    Your shell can complete the commands and man can show them:

    bash
    docenta completions zsh --install     # the script, and a manual page per command
man docenta-search
docenta help --man layers status      # one page, without installing

    --install writes the completion script where the shell loads completions from (fish and bash-completion load their own folders; for zsh, PowerShell and elvish it goes under ~/.docenta/completions and the one line to add to your shell's configuration is printed) and the manual pages under ~/.local/share/man/man1. It edits no configuration file. The onboarding does this for the shell it is run from, and every update rewrites what is installed, so a new build's commands complete the day it arrives.

    An agent that works through a shell can be given skills/docenta-cli/SKILL.md from the repository: the same contract and every command, written by the build (docenta dev skill).

    5.8 What gets indexed: the inclusion policy#

    Docenta walks everything under its roots and keeps a record of every file it saw; what it does NOT record is decided by one policy, applied identically on the walker lane (macOS, Linux) and the NTFS lane (the UFFS producer on Windows). The policy is a precedence ladder, top rule wins:

    1. Store roots and other accounts' homes - docenta's own data,
      2. index and staging directories, and every sibling of your home under the users directory. Never indexed; not configurable.
    2. Config exclude globs ([discovery].excludes) - the hygiene set:
      3. .git, node_modules, package caches, a project's vendor/ tree, application bundles (**/*.app/Contents), editor extension stores (**/.vscode/extensions and its Insiders and Cursor siblings, **/JetBrains/*/plugins), browser and OS caches, trash and system reserves, an Obsidian vault's .obsidian and .trash, and the operating system's own trees, anchored at the volume root: on macOS /usr, /opt, /System, /Library (the system library; ~/Library with Mail and Messages stays in), /bin, /sbin, /private, /etc, /var, /tmp, /cores, /dev, /nix; on Linux /usr, /opt, /etc, the system parts of /var (/var/mail, /var/spool and /var/www stay in), /proc, /sys, /dev, /run, /boot, /lib, /lib64, /lib32, /bin, /sbin, /snap, /nix, /tmp, /lost+found; on Windows, on every fixed drive, \Windows, \Program Files, \Program Files (x86), \ProgramData, \Recovery, \PerfLogs, \MSOCache, \Intel, \AMD, \NVIDIA. Gitignore syntax; a bare name matches a whole directory component at any depth, **/a/b a pair, and a leading / anchors at the root of the volume being walked - /usr is the system's /usr, never a project folder named usr, and a --root inside a pruned tree still walks it. Setting the key replaces the whole list; [discovery].exclude_also ADDS to the list in effect instead (the same syntax), the key for one machine's own exclusions
    • a tool's bookkeeping tree, a mirror - without writing the built-in
      • list out and freezing it against the next build's defaults.
    1. Directories proven by what is inside them - a marker-qualified
      2. name ([discovery].qualified_excludes): target holding Cargo's CACHEDIR.TAG, so a customer folder named target is indexed; and, built in, a git object store by its shape: a HEAD file beside objects/ and refs/, whatever the directory is named - a bare clone, a --separate-git-dir, the per-project stores a repo checkout keeps under .repo/project-objects/<name>.git. The history is the git lane's, rendered commit by commit; the packfiles, hook samples and reflogs are never content. docenta why names the proof. The same rules decide which repositories the git lane renders: a clone under an excluded tree (/opt/homebrew's own history, a node_modules dependency) is not rendered, and a folder admit lets in is - the lane reads the pass's config file.
    2. .docentaignore crumbs - your per-directory policy, in gitignore
      3. syntax, evaluated nearest-first and OUTRANKING the .gitignore beside it. An empty crumb hides its whole subtree (the privacy crumb); a crumb with patterns excludes what they name; and a !pattern line un-ignores something the repo's .gitignore hides - the way to keep a gitignored quarantine of design documents in the corpus:
    # UltraFastFileSearch/.docentaignore
!_trash/
!_trash/**

    Both lines, because git semantics judge every path component on its own: when the repo's rule is /_trash/* it names the children, so whitelisting the directory alone leaves them ignored. docenta why on a file inside says which line decided.

    1. .gitignore chains ([discovery].respect_gitignore, on by
      2. default) - what git ignores, docenta ignores, unless a crumb or an include says otherwise. Build outputs and dependency trees stay out without any configuration. Nothing vanishes in silence: every folder or file the chain hides is recorded as an admit gap with the ignored reason, the ignore file and the pattern, and docenta status --waiting lists it. A person's .env, a notes folder or a data/exports tree that the repository ignores is admitted with [discovery].includes, gitignore-syntax patterns anchored at the ingested root that win over every .gitignore:
    toml
    [discovery]
includes = [".env", "notes", "data/exports/**"]

    A pattern with a literal head (data/exports/**) reaches into the ignored data folder above it, and the folder's other children stay ignored; a pattern that starts with ** (**/.env) admits the file wherever its own folder is walked. The crumb's !pattern is the per-directory spelling of the same thing. docenta why names the include that admitted a file.

    Admitted folders ([discovery].admit, new 2026-10-13) lift one folder past rungs 2, 3 and 5 - an exclude pattern, a marker, a .gitignore - by its absolute path (~/ for the home folder):

    toml
    [discovery]
admit = ["~/Projects/vendor/manuals", "E:\\Web\\Hardware\\node_modules\\pkg"]

    The folder itself is entered and the rules still judge what is inside it (a node_modules inside an admitted folder stays out). A folder above it that the policy prunes is entered as a passage only: its other entries stay out. Rungs 1 and 4 are never lifted: the store's own data and other accounts' homes stay out, and an empty crumb outranks an admit (remove the crumb instead). The walk, the change stream, the NTFS lane (its producer stops pruning the pattern at enumeration and the consumer judges) and docenta why read the same list. docenta setup scope writes it: the let-in button beside a folder the policy keeps out.

    1. The NTFS name prune ([discovery].name_excludes) - file names
      2. the Windows producer never enumerates: extension-less non-content such as .dirstamp, uevent, __data, manifest-*. Note the matcher: | alternation, case-folded, a bare literal matches as a SUBSTRING, a pattern with * or ? as the whole name - so never put lock or master there.

    Whatever survives the ladder is recorded. Files docenta cannot read (binaries without an extension, formats no lane handles) keep a metadata row - the record that it looked - and are never re-read until they change.

    To know what the policy decided for one file, ask:

    bash
    docenta why "/Users/me/Github/UltraFastFileSearch/_trash/docs/design.md"

    path    : /Users/me/Github/UltraFastFileSearch/_trash/docs/design.md
stored  : no
verdict : included (crumb whitelist)
reason  : whitelisted by "!_trash/" in /Users/me/Github/UltraFastFileSearch/.docentaignore (the crumb outranks the .gitignore beside it)

    --json gives the same as a record. The MCP check_path tool reports the same reason in not_stored_because. The rule the two enforcement points must agree on is pinned by a test that feeds every default glob through both spellings.

    6. Bringing in more than files#

    Files on disk are only part of your life. These surfaces bring in the rest. All of them work the same way: material is rendered into ordinary email files in a staging area called the *spool* (~/.docenta/spool), and then ingested as normal content. Nothing invents a special storage format.

    6.1 AI chats#

    bash
    docenta status --sources     # every source, its state, and the command that brings it in

    status changes nothing. It lists each source docenta knows, for example:

    SOURCE    MODE      STATE                                    COMMAND
claude    dynamic   55 sessions under ~/.claude/projects     docenta ingest claude
chatgpt   snapshot  nothing dropped yet                      docenta ingest chatgpt <export.zip>
claude-ai snapshot  no export ingested yet                   docenta ingest claude-ai <manifest.json>

    Two kinds of source:

    • Dynamic - Claude Code and Codex sessions and Zed's agent threads are
      • found on your machine and need nothing from you: docenta ingest claude, docenta ingest codex, docenta ingest zed. The hourly sync picks up new ones by itself.
    • Snapshot - ChatGPT requires *you* to export, because docenta cannot log
      • in as you. On chatgpt.com: Settings, Data controls, Export data. OpenAI mails a download link that expires in 24 hours. Then:
    bash
    docenta ingest chatgpt ~/Downloads/<the export>.zip

    It unpacks the archive safely, remembers it by its fingerprint so a re-run costs nothing, and refuses an archive that tries to escape its folder. The [chats] transcript word applies here too: under full the model's thoughts and every tool's output (a code cell's result, a browse result) are turns of their own; prose, the default, keeps the conversation. The files in the export come along: what you uploaded (under its own name), the images it generated and your voice recordings are placed beside the conversations, so a photo you sent is read like any other photo and a PDF you uploaded is searchable. Drop a later export beside an earlier one and each conversation renders from the copy updated last; an export you unzipped yourself can be dropped as a folder.

    • Snapshot, the Claude apps - the chats you have on claude.ai, in the
      • desktop app and on the phone live in your Claude account, not on your machine, so they come home the same way. On claude.ai: Settings, Privacy, Export data. Claude mails a small *manifest* file that names one download link per part of the export (conversations, projects, design chats, pages you published, account records). Save the manifest, then:
    bash
    docenta ingest claude-ai ~/Downloads/manifest-<...>.json

    For every part that is not yet beside the manifest, docenta opens its link in *your own* browser, which must be signed in to claude.ai, and waits for the file to land in the same folder. It downloads nothing itself: the links only answer a signed-in browser, and each works once. You can also point the command at a folder holding the ZIP files, or at one already unpacked. Every conversation is rendered, an edited prompt's other branch as a document of its own; so is every project with its documents, every design chat, and every page you published with all its versions.

    Note

    The raw export is kept beside the renders so the hourly pass can render it again, but it is never indexed as it is: an empty .docentaignore sits in that folder, and what is searchable is what is rendered from it. Everything in it is: every folder level is read, and a file the lane has no special shape for (your account record, your login history, anything else a category carries) renders as a record of its own, its fields on one line each. A conversation the export lists without a single word in it is counted and skipped; the command says how many.

    6.2 Messenger chats#

    Separate command, same machinery, different category: messenger chats are ordinary documents, NOT part of the chats scope (which holds AI agent sessions only). Search them unscoped, or by their path.

    bash
    docenta ingest whatsapp --status     # what is in the drop box, nothing ingested
docenta ingest whatsapp              # harvest the drop, render and ingest

    WhatsApp needs a local iPhone backup: create one on this Mac, materialize the WhatsApp app-group subtree (iMazing, WhatsApp-Chat-Exporter, or chat4n6 all work), and drop the subtree - or a .zip of it containing ChatStorage.sqlite - into ~/.docenta/drops/whatsapp. Docenta reads that database read-only, checks the schema before touching it, and renders one message file per chat-month. A photo, a voice note, a document, a location or a contact card is rendered as what it is (the file's name and caption, the coordinates, the card), and when the subtree carries the media files they are placed beside the chats, so a photo you were sent is read like any other. In a group chat every message names the member who sent it. For a named store (docenta --store NAME ingest whatsapp) the drop folder is NAME.docenta-drops/whatsapp beside the store, and the renders land in that store's own spool.

    6.3 Mail#

    Two routes, and you can use both:

    1. Files you already have. Any .mbox, .eml, or .msg in a folder you
      2. ingest is picked up, and so is a mailbox that carries no extension: a mailbox is recognised by how it opens (an envelope line, then a header line), so Thunderbird's folders (Inbox, Sent, Archives under the profile's Mail/<server>/) and an Apple Mail export (Name.mbox/mbox) count the same as a .mbox. Large mailboxes explode into one searchable item per message automatically; a mailbox over the 256 MB ceiling prints a note and waits for you to run docenta ingest mailbox explicitly. When you answered on to the archives question at onboarding, a mailbox that grows later (a Thunderbird folder, a fresh export at the same path) is exploded again on the next pass, and only its new messages are read.
    2. Live IMAP. One command, once, at the keyboard:
    bash
    docenta setup mail

    The address this machine already knows is offered before you type: on the page as the pre-filled value (the others it knows as the field's suggestions), at the terminal as the Enter default (the others listed). Where it looks, in order: the accounts docenta already keeps up to date here, then the mail clients installed on this machine - Apple Mail (the addresses its inbox is delivered to), Thunderbird and Evolution (their identities). Never a git identity: a noreply address is no mailbox. Change it or take it.

    (docenta setup mail starts the docenta-mail-setup program of this install: the page and the Google sign-in are the two things in docenta that listen on an address, and they live outside the program that reads your files. A hardened install can leave that binary out.)

    A page opens in your browser with four numbered steps in plain words: your address; switching on the provider's 2-Step Verification (a button opens the page); making the key on the provider's page, click by click (Gmail, Apple and Yahoo all issue one; it is a separate password for one program, and you can throw it away any time); pasting it into a box. The page is served by docenta on your own computer and only once: what you paste goes into the operating system's credential store - the macOS Keychain, the Windows Credential Manager, the Linux keyring - and nowhere else. --cli-only gives the same four steps in the terminal window, with a pause after each. Nothing secret is written to any file.

    Not now. Every way through has a way out that changes nothing: the page's "Not now" button, Enter in the terminal window while the page waits, or skip at either terminal prompt. The setup ends with "skipped for now", onboarding records the mail question as later, and docenta setup mail opens the page again any time. A provider the page does not know (no Gmail, Apple or Yahoo steps to show) gets a "Mail server" field on the page: name the server the provider's own help page gives for IMAP, paste the app password, and the login is proven the same way; or choose Not now. It then writes the connector settings (~/.docenta/spool-state/imap.toml, which names the account and the command that reads the secret back), proves one login, and from then on every scheduled pass brings the mailbox current.

    Every folder. docenta asks the server for its folders (once a day) and fetches every one: Inbox, Sent, Archive, Junk and every folder you made. On Gmail, whose "All Mail" already holds your inbox, your sent mail and every label, it fetches All Mail, Spam, Trash and Drafts; your labels arrive on each message. The login check lists the folders it will keep current. To fetch fewer, name them in imap.toml (mailboxes = ["INBOX", "Sent"]); mailboxes = ["*"] on an account means every folder again. A machine set up before this keeps the list the setup used to write (["[Gmail]/All Mail", "[Gmail]/Trash"] on Gmail, ["INBOX"] elsewhere); docenta reads exactly those lists as no setting and fetches every folder without a new setup, says so once in the pass's log, and docenta status --sources shows it on the imap row. Any other list is yours and is kept. Outlook.com is refused with the reason: Microsoft accepts no password over IMAP any more.

    A Google account has two ways in, kept apart on the page: Sign in with Google comes first and is the way; the app password is folded away under it as "Use an app password instead", and a question inside a folded path is not asked. The sign-in uses docenta's own Google client, built into the binary the way every desktop program carries one; an operator who brings a client of their own stores it with docenta setup mail --google-client ID:SECRET (a Desktop-app client from the Google Cloud console with the scope https://mail.google.com/) and that one wins. A build made without a built-in client says so on the page and offers the app password until a client is stored. Every other provider has the app password only. With the button, the page shows "Sign in with Google" and docenta setup mail --google does the same in the terminal: a Google window opens, you choose the account and click Allow, and the window says you may close it. What Google hands back (a refresh token) goes into the credential store like a key, and docenta renews its access before every fetch. While the app is not yet verified by Google the window shows an "app not verified" warning; Advanced, then Go to docenta, continues. The permission is taken away at myaccount.google.com/permissions, and docenta says so at the next fetch.

    The cost, before anything is fetched. The login check also sizes the account: the message count of each mailbox, and its size from the sizes of the newest 200 messages (read from the server's own list, no message is downloaded), extrapolated over the count. A time is given only from a rate this machine measured: every scheduled fetch records the bytes its body session landed and how long it took, and once at least 1 MB over at least a second has moved, the setup says "about N h over IMAP at this machine's measured rate". On a machine that never fetched mail it says no rate is measured yet and gives no time. The verdict: a history that takes more than four hours over IMAP is large (without a rate, more than 10 GB is); a large one is steered to a mailbox dump first - request a Google Takeout (Mail, mbox), bring it in with docenta ingest mailbox <file>, then docenta setup mail --anchor, so the hourly pass only tops off from the dump's newest date (the mail anchor); docenta schedule pause keeps the pass from starting the whole pull meanwhile.
