A small one is fetched by the next hourly pass, or at once with docenta update --only imap. Onboarding's mail hand-off records the sizing and the advice in the ledger's mail row. The server's quota is not used: on Gmail it is the whole Google storage, Drive and Photos included.

    The hand-off from a Google Takeout: ingest the export first (route 1), and the ingest offers this step at once, with the export's own address prefilled. The export records how far it reached (the mail anchor) and whose mail it is (the address its messages were delivered to), and the live fetch of THAT account starts from there, not from the beginning. Every other account fetches its whole history: a Takeout of one account never shortens another's. If the export's messages name no address, or you set the account up by hand, docenta setup mail --anchor (or use_mail_anchor = true in imap.toml) says the export is this account's; use_mail_anchor = false always fetches the whole history. docenta schedule status says whether mail is live or a top-up is waiting.

    A machine with a password manager may still point imap.toml at it by hand (password_command = "gopass show -o docenta/gmail-app-password"); the setup command leaves such an entry alone and adds its account beside it.

    The fetch uses your system curl over IMAPS. It never deletes or modifies anything in your mailbox. A message whose download fails is kept on a retry list in the account's cursor and tried again on every following pass until it lands or the server no longer has it; the pass's summary names it (RETRY 1: uid 4711). A download has sixty seconds plus one second per 16 KiB of the message's size (a 100 MB attachment gets about 1 h 45 min), so a large message on a slow link is given the time it needs rather than dropped.

    6.4 Git history#

    bash
    docenta ingest git              # every repository under your home, now
docenta ingest git --root DIR   # every repository under DIR
docenta update --only git       # the same, as the step of the pass

    Every git repository the scope's walk admits is ingested end to end: a clone of someone else's project counts the same as your own work (a repository in your pile is your data). Repositories are found at any depth; only the exclusion policy's hygiene set (caches, build output, package trees, app bundles, editor stores) and cloud-synced mounts are not entered. Bare repositories and initialized submodules are included. The lane does not walk your disks to find them: the store already knows every folder a scanned file sits in, and the git step checks those folders for a repository (one look each, <data>/git/candidates.json is the list) before the spool binary renders them. A store with nothing scanned yet is the one case the roots are walked.

    Every commit renders as one item: every commit of every author on every branch and tag (not only the checked-out line), with the full message (never cut), the author and the committer with both dates, the parents, the refs that point at it, and every changed path with its added and deleted line counts. There is no cap on the commit count: the log is streamed off git, and after each repository its tips are recorded, so the first pass renders the whole history and every pass after it only the commits new since the recorded tips (a rewritten branch whose old tip is gone falls back to the whole history once; the renders are idempotent). The history lives in the chats spool under git/, one .eml per commit, so "why did we change this, and when" is a search, and search --scopes git keeps to the commits.

    One repository, one history. A linked work tree (git worktree add) shares its main work tree's refs, so only the main one renders. Clones of one remote share a tag (the origin URL's repository name; a repository without a remote keeps its directory name), so a commit both hold is one item and a commit only one clone holds still renders from that clone. A commit's item is written once and never rewritten: its ref decoration is a snapshot of the moment it was rendered. A render whose tag belongs to no repository any more (a removed work tree, a clone that learned its remote) is removed on the next pass and retired from the index with it; the step's summary says N orphaned renders removed. A store built before 2026-10-11 may hold such duplicates (the owner's Mac had 24,061 items for 13,304 commits); its next docenta update removes them.

    Your own addresses are a facet, never a filter. The lane learns them from git config user.email and user.name (global and per repository) and from the histories themselves (every address a commit carries under a name you are known by), and records them in ~/.docenta/spool-state/git_identities.json:

    json
    { "addresses": ["me@example.org", "me@old-job.example"],
  "names": ["My Name"], "not": [] }

    Add an address by editing that file (or by setting DOCENTA_GIT_AUTHORS=a@x,b@y for one run); put one under not to keep it out for good. The addresses join your mail addresses for direction: sent, so search --scopes git --direction sent is "my own commits".

    A store built before 2026-10-09 holds zero commits of the repositories the old authorship rule skipped; its next docenta update renders the whole history (the summary's "came along" line says how many commits).

    Into another store (a foreign history as a corpus of its own): docenta --store NAME ingest git --root DIR renders into that store's own spool beside it, never into the machine's.

    6.5 OCR: making scans readable#

    Images and scanned PDFs hold text no search can reach until it is extracted. Docenta does this in a separate producer so your search engine never waits on it:

    bash
    # 1. run the producer (long-running; safe to stop and restart)
docenta update --only produce

# 2. fold the results into search (fast - about a minute for tens of thousands)
docenta update --only analysis

    Every update pass runs both steps, so this is only for doing it now. The producer is code in docenta that runs as a process of its own (docenta __program docenta-analysis, with the store's analysis folder, its state database read-only and the OCR models), so a pass that reads pictures cannot take the process that answers down with it.

    After that, a scanned invoice ranks by the words printed on it. Files that are cloud placeholders (0 bytes locally) are skipped: no bytes, no text.

    6.6 Moving material between your own machines#

    A bale is one archive of your rendered chats and git history, digest- manifested so tampering is detected:

    bash
    docenta store export ~/mymachine.bale.zip
docenta store import ~/mymachine.bale.zip --ingest    # on the other machine

    Import verifies every member before landing any of them; a tampered bale lands nothing. Identical files are skipped, so re-importing is free.

    Note

    Mail is deliberately never included unless you ask for it by name with --lanes.

    6.7 A whole collection in a bale, ready to use#

    A bale of a store (docenta store export, or docenta store ship for a named collection) carries everything that was expensive to make: the extracted text, the search terms, and the meaning-vectors together with the search graph built over them, packed as finished *segments*. The machine that imports it builds nothing of that again. It unpacks the segments and takes them in as they are, so a collection of millions of passages is ready in the minutes it takes to copy it, on a small old laptop as on anything else. Only the word index and the people-and-places layers are made locally, by one docenta layers pipeline run, and that needs no graphics card.

    Three things follow from a collection arriving as its own segments:

    • It is called what it is. A collection keeps its own name wherever it
      • lands (sleep, not the computer that built it). Where and when it was cut is recorded beside the name, and docenta store imports shows both.
    • It stays itself. The segments of an imported collection are *locked*:
      • your own store's housekeeping never merges them with your own material or with another collection. You can hold several (a sleep-research library, a law library) side by side.
    • A newer bale replaces the older one of the same origin as whole
      • segments, without touching anything else.
    • It leaves as one piece. docenta store forget-import LABEL --yes removes the
      • collection's files and its segments at once; nothing is left to clean up.

    When you export only *part* of a store (one folder, or the public part of a store that also holds private material), docenta builds fresh segments for exactly that part while exporting, so nothing that was not selected can travel along, and the importing machine still builds nothing.

    Note

    A bale written by this version is format 3. An older docenta refuses it with "upgrade docenta" rather than importing it without its vectors; this version still imports older bales the old way.

    7. Keeping it fresh automatically#

    Ingesting once is not the point; staying current is. One command runs the whole live spine, and a second registers it with whatever scheduler this machine already has.

    7.0 One pass, three stages: docenta update (new)#

    Note

    New in the CLI arc's first phase (2026-10-09). The verbs it gathers are its STEPS, named with --only: stale, finish, recover and analysis were ingest verbs of their own until the arc's third phase retired them (2026-10-09), and the store's derivative verbs (backfill, enrich, promote-bodies, reindex, expire) followed the same day: each is update --only STEP, expire also tidy --only expire; the semantic sibling's prune and repair verbs followed (update --only prune|repair), and the scheduled pass is update --scheduled itself. docenta layers pipeline stays as the semantic stage alone.

    docenta update runs everything that keeps a store current, in one pass and three stages, from the answers given at onboarding (the capability ledger, the lane word and its turbo consent, the recorded scope):

    1. ingest: backfill (a pre-bundle store only), the scan over the
      2. roots the store was given, recover, finish, stale, chats, imap, explode (the mailbox archives, on the word given), produce (OCR, by the ledger), analysis, enrich, promote-bodies (once per build), reindex (only when the search index predates this build's schema), expire (the absence hold's end and the per-pass gc).
    2. semantic: repair (once per repair generation), the unit-index
      3. reset only when the index predates a field, the pipeline to the feed head within the lane word and its consent.
    3. tidy: docenta tidy --auto - the reclaim without the walk when
      4. the compaction is due by the coverage threshold (gc, the semantic prune, the compaction, the catch-up, the semantic compact, the stack once more), else the semantic prune and the final layer check; always on an update you type, by threshold on a scheduled one (section 8.0). gc and the compaction alone when named.

    While it runs it holds THIS store's schedule (a marker under the store's data root, released when it ends, on an error too), so the hourly job of this store stands down and no other store's job notices. It is quiet by default:

    text
    ingest     : 11 steps ran in 1 s (scan 1 s, recover 0 s, ...); 3 skipped (backfill, imap, reindex)
semantic   : 1 step ran in 0 s (pipeline 0 s); 4 skipped (repair, prune, reset-units, tail-windows)
tidy       : 1 step ran in 0 s (tidy 0 s); 2 skipped (gc, compact)
came along : content objects 20 (unchanged); file instances 20 (unchanged); sessions rendered 0 (Claude Code 0, Codex 0)
layers     : all 5 current
not counted: changed files, OCR pages, mail fetched - each step's own numbers are in the transcript (`-v` streams them)
embed      : current - nothing to embed; the next delta is measured at the line
line       : under the turbo word, or with no word on record, a delta projected under 2 h 0 min at this machine's measured rate is built here instead of shipped or asked (sparse terms, dense vectors and code vectors alike); over it the turbo word ships all three lanes inside the consent and no word asks. The line never applies under later (both lanes wait for a word) or lazy (what is asked about is embedded first). Rates: ...
done       : update complete in 2 s (transcript: /tmp/arc1/after/store/logs/sync.log)

    (A frozen 20-file scratch store on 2026-10-09; the stage lines of a real store carry the minutes.)

    -v streams every step's own output as the pass always has. The "came along" numbers are measured before and after the run, never read off a child's prose; what this build does not count says so.

    bash
    docenta update                      # the three stages, by hand
docenta update -v                   # every step streamed
docenta update --stage semantic     # one stage alone
docenta update --only stale --only pipeline   # named steps; a step the plan skips by default runs when named
docenta update --scheduled          # what the scheduler's job runs: nothing asked, turbo only inside the consent, tidy by threshold

    The step names --only takes: backfill, scan, recover, finish, stale, chats, imap, explode, produce, analysis, enrich, promote-bodies, reindex, expire, repair, prune, reset-units, pipeline, tail-windows, gc, compact, tidy. A step the plan leaves out of a default run (gc, which the expire step already ran; promote-bodies under a build that judged the bodies already; prune and tail-windows, which the pipeline's own steps cover) runs when named. A step that CANNOT run (OCR deferred at onboarding, a sibling binary not installed) is said and stays skipped.

    The local line, stated, and when it applies. Under the turbo word, or with no word on record, a delta the pipeline projects under two hours at this machine's measured rate is built here instead of shipped or asked - sparse terms, dense vectors and code vectors alike. That is what the line is for: the turbo word ships only a delta OVER it, so a few thousand units never go to a GPU, and the summary prints both the line and the rates it is measured against. The line never applies under later (both lanes wait for your word; nothing embeds and nothing is encoded, however small the delta) or lazy (what you ask about is embedded first, the rest waits): those words hold the lanes until another word replaces them, an unattended run leaves them alone, and a run in a terminal offers the word as the default and asks again. --embed turbo at an onboarding whose every lane projects short says so on the spot: both lanes run here, nothing is quoted or sent, and a later delta over the line is asked for turbo again.

    The scheduled pass is the same plan. docenta update --scheduled is a projection of the update's step table under the scheduled posture, so the two never drift; the scheduler's command moves to docenta update --scheduled in a later phase of the arc.

    7.0.1 One page: docenta status (new)#

    Note

    New in the CLI arc's first phase (2026-10-09). stats, docenta layers status, schedule status and docenta setup runtime remain beside it until their group of the arc's third phase lands; each is a flag of this page. The source map, the pre-approved queue and the maintenance journal (the former ingest and store verbs) are status --sources, status --waiting and status --progress alone since 2026-10-09.

    docenta status is one page: the store (objects, instances, families, the seal or the hold), every semantic layer with its percentage and the vectors it holds, the pending dense work with the basis of the measure and the rate it is timed at (the last embed pass of the model on this machine, or the record's probe until one has run), the code partition's own line (its pending count and lane state, or "no code model installed"), the standing turbo consent, the sync (installed, cadence, next run, the last pass, a pause or a hold), and what the next update would do, stage by stage, from a read-only plan. Nothing on it is a second implementation: the semantic lines are docenta-semantic status --json read back, the store lines the stats reader's, the plan the update's own.

    text
    sealed          : no
store      : 54 content objects, 55 file instances (text 50, document 3, image 1)
layer      : unit-index                                  75.9%
layer      : dense:arctic-embed-m-v2.0@snowflake-95c2741    75.9%  held 40
layer      : mentions                                    75.9%
layer      : entities                                   100.0%
layer      : gazetteer                                  100.0%
layers     : 3 of 5 behind
pending    : 13 units to embed (counted on the feed tail)
consent    : you consented to 0.5 GPU-hours (turbo consent, 100 texts and 100 units, 2026-10-09); 0.0 shipped on it, 0.5 left, 0.1 of allowance for growth between passes; an unattended pass ships only inside that and asks beyond it
sync       : NOT installed for the store at /tmp/arc1/after/store (`docenta schedule on`); last pass 0 s ago
next update: ingest    runs scan, recover, finish, stale, chats, explode, produce, analysis, enrich, expire; skips backfill, imap, promote-bodies, reindex
next update: semantic  runs pipeline; skips repair, prune, reset-units, tail-windows
next update: tidy      runs nothing; skips gc, compact, tidy (the scheduled pass)
next update: tidy      runs tidy; skips gc, compact (a `docenta update` you run)

    (A scratch store on 2026-10-09 whose word is turbo with a pack waiting for consent, so three layers sit behind. A stage both postures plan alike prints one next update line; where the scheduled pass and a docenta update you run differ, each gets a line naming its posture: the scheduled pass tidies by threshold, a docenta update you run tidies always, and its line is the one docenta update --dry-run prints.)

    bash
    docenta status                 # the page
docenta status --json          # the page as one object (store, layers, pending, consent, sync, next_update, next_update_by_hand)
docenta status --content       # the full content table (`stats`)
docenta status --semantic      # the semantic layer page in its own words (`docenta layers status`)
docenta status --sources       # every ingest source, its mode and state (the source map)
docenta status --waiting [FAMILY]   # the files awaiting their extractor lane (the pre-approved queue; --limit N rows)
docenta status --progress      # what the last long-running command is doing (the maintenance journal)
docenta status --runtime       # the ONNX runtime and its lanes (`docenta setup runtime`)

    7.0.2 The answers: docenta setup answers (new)#

    Note

    New in the CLI arc's first phase (2026-10-09); the ledger verb it merged (capabilities) was retired in the third phase the same day.

    The questions onboarding asks up front - OCR, the mailbox archives, a mail account, the agents, the lane word - and the two choices the config holds (the chats transcript, the JSON reading) are one answer set. docenta setup answers shows it: the capability ledger with each row's why, the lane word with its record, the standing turbo consent, the chats transcript and the JSON reading. At a terminal it then asks each question again with the current answer as the default (Enter keeps it) - on a page beside the terminal when a browser can be opened, as onboarding and the mail setup do (below), at the terminal otherwise or under --cli-only; a script sees the table and nothing waits on it.

    bash
    docenta setup answers                       # show; at a terminal, ask again on the page beside it (the terminal when no browser opens)
docenta setup answers --cli-only            # ask again at this terminal, never on a page
docenta setup answers --page                # insist on the page (below); --fresh discards an interrupted edit's draft
docenta setup answers --set ocr=on          # one answer without a terminal: ocr=on|later|off
docenta setup answers --set mbox=now        # mbox=now|later (the archives), mail=now|later, agents=now|later
docenta setup answers --set chats=full      # chats=prose|full, json=records|whole (the config's two choices)
docenta setup answers --set embed=turbo     # embed=local|turbo|lazy|later (the lane word, for every lane: sparse, dense and code)
docenta setup answers --reset               # forget every answer, the consent included; the next build asks fresh
docenta setup answers --json

    The page behaves as the onboarding page does: every toggle on the page prints in the terminal as it is made, the page's button hands the set to the terminal, and Enter in the terminal takes over - each question is asked there with the word the page shows as the default, a typed word shows on the page, a click on the page answers the question the terminal is on - and the final list waits for your Enter before anything is recorded (q keeps it as a draft). The agents found on this machine are ticks under the agents question, an agent whose config already carries docenta ticked and marked connected (the question then reads connected, as the mail question does for an account kept up to date); now with ticks connects the ticked ones right after the record. A mail account connected on the page is recorded. The page's draft (<data dir>/answers-draft.json) survives an interruption: the next run offers the changes not yet on record once (continue, or f for fresh; --fresh decides unasked) and the draft goes when they are recorded.

    It writes RECORDS only - the ledger, the lane records, the config keys - and says what applies them: the next docenta update applies this for OCR, the archives, the chats transcript and the lane word (the produce, explode, chats and pipeline steps read them); docenta setup mail and docenta agents add for the two hand-offs it records but cannot run; docenta setup answers --set json=records|whole for the JSON files already in (new files follow the setting at the next update). Whatever the reading, not every JSON file grows vectors. Each is judged once, at extraction, by what it IS: a *sidecar* (a .json beside a photo or video with the same stem, as Google Takeout writes one per photo) has its facts folded into that file's own record - the description becomes the photo's title, the people, the place and the taken time join its searchable metadata - and grows no vectors itself; a *manifest* or lockfile by its name (package.json, vcpkg.json, tsconfig.*.json, *.lock.json) is a program's wherever it lives; the rest is read by *shape*: sentences among its string values make it prose, which is embedded, while ids, hashes, numbers, paths and timestamps make it a program's output, kept for keyword search only. Where a file sits (app state, caches, package and build trees, the system's folders) stays the last tier, and [storage] unembedded_json still sets whole folders aside by hand. The report under json names each tier with its largest folders and counts the files not judged yet (rows from before this rule; the next update judges them as it re-reads). --set embed=turbo is a word given by hand: the next pass packs and sends inside the standing consent and holds beyond it with the numbers - with no consent on record it holds, as the consent ceiling of 2026-10-09 says.

    7.0.3 The scope, folder by folder: docenta setup scope (new)#

    Note

    New 2026-10-13: the census, the measured mode and the let-in lever ([discovery] admit) the same day.

    What docenta reads and what it costs, on a page: the scope's folder tree, each folder with its files, bytes and kinds (the heaviest extensions with their share), its projected text, sparse and dense units, and beside it, in grey, the folders the policy keeps out with the rule that decided (the same words docenta why gives, for a directory). Small folders fold into their parent and the parent says how many; --depth N keeps more levels. The figures come from one walk of the scope under the ingest's own policy and the preflight sample's per-extension rates (so many bytes of .csv yield so many units), the hours from this machine's probed rates and the relay's rented rate; a pass measures them.

    Every folder has a state - full (read, indexed, embedded), keyword (read and indexed, no vectors: found by its words, not by meaning), off (not read) - set on the folder or inherited from the one above; the totals bar follows every tick (files, bytes, text, units, hours here, GPU-hours rented). A folder already keyword-only starts that way and names the [storage] unembedded entry. The submit hands the set folders to the terminal, which writes the policy and says each line:

    • off: an empty .docentaignore crumb in the folder (the walk never
      • enters it; docenta why names the crumb; remove the file to undo). A folder that cannot take a crumb gets a volume-anchored pattern in [discovery] exclude_also instead, the built-in list left as it is; the line says so.
    • keyword: the folder added to [storage] unembedded.
    • full on a folder that setting named: the entry removed (an entry
      • naming a folder above it is said, not narrowed).
    • let in, beside a folder the policy keeps out: the folder added to
      • [discovery] admit (an exclude pattern, a marker or a .gitignore kept it out), or its own empty crumb removed. A folder kept out by the store's own data, another account's home, or a crumb with patterns above it has no button; the line says why. Off on an admitted folder removes its admit entry instead of writing a crumb.

    The page writes policy and nothing else: the walk, the change stream, the NTFS lane and docenta why read the same entries, and docenta why PATH names the one that decided. The next docenta update walks the new scope; vectors already built for a folder now keyword-only stay until docenta tidy. A folder below a keyword-only one cannot be set full (the setting has no negation). A folder let in shows its cost in the next census.

    Measured, not projected, where the store already knows. When the store holds files under the scope, each folder's text is the store's own count of the characters each extraction kept (a content stored in several places counts once; a file the policy now keeps out is skipped and counted on the store line - the backlog docenta tidy retires). The units follow from that text at the sample's rate per kind, and only the bytes the store does not hold yet are projected. The page shows each folder's measured share; --projected sets the store aside.

    bash
    docenta setup scope                         # the store's recorded scope, on the page beside the terminal; Enter leaves the policy as it is
docenta setup scope --root ~/Dropbox        # one folder
docenta setup scope --preset machine        # every fixed volume
docenta setup scope --cli-only              # the report here; the page written as a file to look at, nothing served
docenta setup scope --json                  # the census: the tree with its figures
docenta setup scope --depth 4
docenta setup scope --projected             # every figure from the sample, the store's counts aside
docenta setup scope --let-in /usr/local/src # the page's let-in from the command line: [discovery] admit, written and said; no page
docenta setup scope --keyword ~/Archive     # keyword-only ([storage] unembedded); --off DIR for off; all three repeatable

    The page is served by docenta-mail-setup --serve-page on this computer only, at a one-time link; the terminal binary opens no socket. The page file is <data dir>/scope/census.html.

    7.0.4 One verdict: docenta doctor (new)#

    Note

    New 2026-11-08, from a field assessment that took eight commands and a reader who knew which line of each mattered.

    docenta doctor is one page of verdicts for this box. It answers at once: the page is the one the last examination wrote, with its age on the last line, while that page is this build's and younger than a pass and a half (the scheduled pass examines at its end). docenta doctor --live examines now, and --fix always examines first. The first line names the host, the user, the store and the build, so a paste from the wrong machine shows itself. Then one line per finding, each OK, INFO, ATTENTION or BLOCKED, with the command that fixes it:

    • PATH: the directory the binaries live in must be on it (the line to
      • add to the shell rc is printed when it is not).
    • The build and the models against the channel: docenta setup check,
      • the channel's signed VERSION against the installed set and the signed index against the models root, nothing else fetched, seconds.
    • The layers: every semantic layer at the feed head, or which are
      • behind and by how much, with the pending units; a parked code pack or an embed waiting for the GPU lane is INFO with docenta cloud ship as the person's word; the query anchor's line when the queries are served from another partition than the configured one.
    • The sync: installed and its cadence, the next run, the last pass; a
      • job an older build registered (docenta schedule migrate); the hand pause; a pass running now; a hold a killed update left behind; every health sentence docenta schedule status prints (cursor lag, a schedule that stopped firing).
    • The turbo jobs: results that landed and are not home (docenta cloud
      • receive), shards to retry, a job still on the lane.
    • Mail: live or not (docenta setup mail), information only.

    The last line counts the attention and blocked findings and says what --fix would run. docenta doctor --fix runs the quick, reversible fixes the page named: the stale hold cleared, docenta schedule on or docenta schedule migrate, docenta setup update, docenta cloud receive. docenta doctor --fix --long adds the one long fix, a by-hand docenta update that catches every layer up (skipped while a pass is running, since that pass is doing the work). A turbo ship is never run by the doctor: the GPU-hours are the person's word, and the ship quotes and asks at the terminal. --json for a tool: it carries live and examined_secs_ago beside the findings.

    docenta setup check is the doctor's question to the channel on its own, read-only; docenta setup verify is the fuller check that fetches the channel's build and runs every binary in it.

    7.1 What the pass does#

    docenta update --scheduled walks these in order, each step resuming from its own cursor so an idle pass costs seconds:

    1. docenta-spool chats - re-render AI chats
      2. the recorded tips (the whole history on the first pass)
    2. docenta-spool imap - bring mail current (it indexes what it fetched)
    3. docenta ingest machine - refresh what the store was given: the folder
      4. onboarding was told, the machine an onboarding without --root walked (the same fixed volumes, the OS trees pruned on both passes), or the roots the ingests recorded (docenta ingest folder DIR, ingest machine --root DIR; a scan without roots records the machine). A store that recorded nothing refreshes nothing on its own, and the pass says so.
    4. docenta update --only analysis - fold in analysis that arrived since last pass
    5. docenta layers pipeline - update every semantic layer

    1a. docenta-spool git - every repository in scope, the commits new since

    There is no separate step to index the spool: the connectors ingest their own output, and the machine-wide scan would pick it up regardless.

    Each step's end is recorded beside the pass transcript, in sync-receipts.json (~/.docenta/ for the default store, <store>/logs/ for a named one): when the step last succeeded and when it last failed. A search that comes back empty reads it to tell "not captured yet" from "not there"; until a pass has written it, capture reads as unknown.

    7.2 Setting it up#

    bash
    docenta schedule on                 # hourly, the default
docenta schedule on --every 240     # a pass every four hours
docenta schedule on --daily-at 03:00  # once a night (a constrained machine)
docenta schedule on --print-units --user svc  # a server: systemd system units to stdout
docenta schedule status                  # installed? paused? when did it last run? every job and its command
docenta schedule migrate [--dry-run]     # rewrite a job an older build registered (see below)
docenta schedule pause                   # maintenance window: passes refuse to run
docenta schedule resume                  # and back
docenta schedule stop                    # end the pass running now; the schedule stays, the next pass continues
docenta schedule off               # stop it again

    A job from before the verb map. The scheduled pass is docenta update --scheduled since 2026-10-09; a job registered by an older build spells the verb that build knew, and that verb is gone without an alias, so such a job would fail every hour. docenta setup update rewrites every docenta job on the machine after the binary swap (section 3.5), and docenta schedule migrate is the same step by hand: the registration text is read back and the one span that holds the command is rewritten to update --scheduled with the store flags it had; the interval or the time of day, the log paths, the PATH and the priority stay byte for byte, and the job is reloaded. --dry-run prints the old and the new command line of each job it would rewrite and changes nothing; -v prints them on the real run too. schedule status lists every docenta job on the machine with its command and marks one still on the old verb OLD COMMAND. A job that is not docenta's is never read.

    A server under a service account. The user timer above needs a login session bus, which a service account has none of. --print-units prints the two systemd system units instead, hardened as far as a pass can bear: the account named, no new privileges, no devices, a private temp, the whole system read-only, every home hidden but the account's own, the data disks hidden but the roots the store recorded (bound read-only) and the store itself (read-write), the network shut when no mail account is configured, low priority. Paths are printed canonical, so a symlinked home names the directory it points to. Root places them under /etc/systemd/system and enables the timer; the lines at the end of the output say exactly that, and a root you add later needs its own BindReadOnlyPaths line. Two things follow from the account being the identity. The device key, the lease and the seal live in that account's ~/.docenta/license, so onboard, license and update as the service account itself (sudo -u svc -H docenta setup onboard --root /srv/vault, sudo -u svc -H docenta setup update); a lease taken by your own account does not carry over. And the pass reads what the account can read: give it read access to the vault and nothing more, and write access only to its home and the store ([storage] data_dir).

    On Linux the device key is a file only the account can read, and docenta license rekey moves it into the machine's TPM 2.0. Nothing moves it there without that command: a new install makes the file key, and a Linux machine is not reminded to move. In the TPM the key is derived inside the chip when a process first needs it and stored nowhere, so a copy of the license folder carried to another machine is a lease without a key. What it takes, and what to know first:

    • The account must be able to open the kernel's TPM device,
      • /dev/tpmrm0. On most systems that is membership of the group tss (sudo usermod -aG tss USER), and it holds for processes started after it was given: log out fully, or reboot, so that the account's background jobs have it too (the renewal job is one of them). Know what the group gives: on a machine whose TPM has no owner password, which is the usual state on Linux, a member can use the whole TPM, clear it included, and a cleared TPM loses whatever else was sealed to it (a disk encryption key, for one). Do not add a service account to it lightly.
    • docenta license rekey makes a key in the TPM, uses it once, and
      • only then moves the license to it. When the TPM does not take the key the command says why (no device, no permission, an owner password, a TPM that will not make such a key) and the file key stays.
    • A scheduled pass that runs under the hardened system unit above
      • cannot see the TPM: PrivateDevices=true hides it, and the pass would run without its license. A machine whose key is in the TPM needs a drop-in for that unit with PrivateDevices=false, DevicePolicy=closed and DeviceAllow=/dev/tpmrm0 rw.
    • The binding is to the machine, not to the account: another account
      • on the same machine that can open the TPM device and read the license folder's device.tag derives the same key. And a virtual machine's TPM is a file of its host, cloned with the machine.
    • A TPM that is cleared, reset by a firmware update, or replaced has
      • another key: docenta says the TPM no longer derives the recorded key, and docenta license rekey --lost carries the license to the new one (one of the three device changes a year).

    The TPM key has been tested against a software TPM and, as of this writing, on no hardware TPM.

    A device key that is gone - a TPM clear, a restore to a new disk, a new motherboard - while the lease is still installed is one command: docenta license rekey --lost. It mints a new key, proves the old identity with the installed lease, and the license service binds the new key to the same license on the spot, carries your turbo credit, grant and job history over and sends the new lease, which the command installs. A license has three such self-service device changes per rolling year. A working software key moved into the hardware keystore is docenta license rekey without the flag: the candidate key is made first, the service binds the license to it, and only then is it recorded, so a refusal leaves the software key as it was; the old private key is shredded, its public half kept as *.previous. Since 2026-10-25 docenta says so itself when the key is a software file and a hardware keystore is reachable: a hint once, a daily reminder from the third day (the agents' status carries it under action_needed), every run from the seventh, and from the fourteenth day the Pro acts (importing bales, importing turbo results) wait until the key has moved; everything local keeps working. On the service side every device change mails the address the device verified for its turbo grant (else the operator) with both device codes, the time and the way back; a license changes device three times a year and once a day; and a lease issued to a software key carries three days of grace instead of seven, so a copied license directory dies sooner. What no measure undoes: a software key is a file, and a copy taken before the move signs until its lease runs out. docenta names the command whenever it finds a lease and no key. On Windows, a licenser run over ssh cannot open the user's TPM keys and says "no device key" although the key is there: check from the machine's own console first.

    7.2.1 Pro's lease: what the renewal is, and is not#

    docenta phones nobody about your data, and Free docenta contacts no service at all: there is no account, no key, no check. Pro is different in one place only. A Pro machine holds a lease, a signed ticket from the license service that says which license this device is on and what it may do; the ticket is good for two days and carries seven days of grace (three for a software key). The renewal job (the licenser program's renew --if-due, installed on the platform scheduler when the license is activated; docenta license schedule status|remove shows and removes it, docenta license renew renews by hand) runs every six hours and does nothing while the ticket has more than a day left, so it renews once a day and has three more tries when a run cannot sign: a Secure Enclave key made before 2026-10-25 signs only while the Mac is unlocked, and a job that fired once a day at a locked hour used to miss every day (keys made since sign after the first unlock since boot; docenta license rekey makes one). When it does renew, it asks for the next ticket with exactly four fields: this device's key hash, the ticket's sequence number, the engine version and a signature over the ticket's nonce. Nothing about your corpus travels: no file names, no counts, no queries, no store sizes, no machine name. docenta license show --last-exchange prints the last request and answer byte for byte so you can see that for yourself. The service learns that the device is alive and which version it runs, and keeps the time of the renewal; that is the whole of it. A fleet license adds the fleet report (section 7.2), a personal license never sends one.

    The ticket is verified here, offline, in twelve steps (docenta license status --explain walks them): the signature against the key manifest, the device binding, the dates against the seal's trusted clock. So a machine without a network keeps its Pro for the two days plus the grace, and an old version keeps running: nothing checks back in. When the grace runs out, the Pro acts (importing bales, landing turbo results) wait until a renewal goes through; every search, ingest and answer on your own machine goes on exactly as before, as Free. There is no kill switch beyond that, by design. docenta license remove takes the lease off and leaves the device key and the seal; the machine is Free docenta from that moment.

    A license has seats: three come with Pro, up to six can be bought on the shop page (one more seat is $25 for the remaining term, or $45 once on a lifetime Pro; past six write to us for a team license). A device takes a seat when it binds (a purchase, a grant code, a provisioning token) and keeps it while it renews. docenta license devices lists the seats from any device on the license, by device code, keystore and last renewal, and says which are live; docenta license release <code> gives a seat back, this machine's own included (its lease then runs out). A dead machine cleans up after itself: a seat whose device has not renewed for longer than a lease lives (two days plus the grace) goes to the next device that binds, the service records the move, mails the address on the license with both device codes, and allows six such moves a year; a live seat is never taken, only released. A machine with Pro for life is told so on the shop page and in docenta license; there is no term to buy for it, and a Pro code redeemed on it is refused unspent.

    A machine that must not talk. Some machines never open a connection: an air-gapped box, a workstation under a strict policy, a server you would rather keep deaf. Pro works there by file, with the same license, seats and prices. On that machine, docenta license request writes a small signed file (its device key, the key's kind, the engine version, the installed lease's number, a time, and the device's signature over all of it; nothing about your data). Carry the file to any browser and open https://license.docenta.ai/license.html: the page checks the signature, shows the device code, and sends you to the shop page for that device, where Pro is bought or a grant code redeemed as for any machine. Back on the license page, the lease file is yours to download: 90 days with 14 days of grace. On the deaf machine, docenta license install <file> verifies it against the built-in root and keeps it; docenta license status then says "a lease by file" beside the date. Before it runs out, write a fresh request file there and come back with it; every download is a new lease, the old one stays good until its date, and the device keeps its seat throughout. The same page takes the ask for what the shop does not sell (a team past six seats, a site, an annual lease by file): your address and a note go to us with the request file, and the lease file comes back by mail, usually within a day. Nothing on the deaf machine ever talks to us; the renewal job of the paragraph above is for machines that do, and a lease by file is left alone by it until its last day.

    pause and resume are the two ends of a maintenance window: compact and docenta tidy --only semantic-compact take the writer lock a scan would contend for, so pause first, run them, resume. The switch is a marker file (~/.docenta/sync.pause) that the pass, the MCP trigger and status all honor. It stops what runs unattended: the scheduled pass and every step it spawns, the pipeline an ingest starts detached. A docenta layers pipeline you start by hand is not a pass: it notes the pause and runs, so an emergency stop of the scan does not cost you the semantic refresh.

    One command, three schedulers: Windows Task Scheduler, macOS launchd, and systemd user timers on Linux. Installing is idempotent, so re-running it after an upgrade re-points the schedule at the new binary.

    One job per store. The schedule is registered per store, and the command decides which: docenta schedule on without --store or --data-dir registers the machine's own store under the label every existing install carries (net.docenta.sync on macOS, the task docenta-sync on Windows, the user timer docenta-sync.timer on Linux); docenta --store legal schedule on registers a job of its own for the named store (net.docenta.sync.legal, docenta-sync-legal), and docenta --data-dir /srv/vault schedule on one for that data dir, told apart by a short stable hash of the directory. Each job's command carries the store flag it was installed with (--store legal or --data-dir /srv/vault before update --scheduled), so a pass reads only its store, and its transcript and error stream live beside that store (<data dir>/logs/ sync.log and sync.err). uninstall removes only the store's own job; status names the store its first line is about and then lists every docenta job on the machine with the store each serves. Onboarding a store into another data dir or under a name registers that store's job and never touches the machine's.

    A store's own pass keeps to that store in its spool steps too. The machine's store renders agent sessions from your home into ~/.docenta/spool and fetches the mail accounts docenta setup mail connected, as it always has. Any other store renders into a spool of its own beside it (<store>.docenta-spool), ingests the renders into itself and no other, and reads the agent sessions about its scope: a store over a folder takes every Claude Code and Codex session whose working directory lies under that folder, from the session roots in your home where the agents keep them (~/.claude/projects, ~/.codex), never the sessions about anything else (a store over the whole machine reads them all). The mail step is the machine store's: another store's pass skips it and says so, and takes mail as an archive (docenta --store NAME ingest mailbox <file>).

    Every pass appends to ~/.docenta/sync.log for the machine's store (a named store's or a data dir's pass appends beside that store), streaming as it goes rather than at the end - a long step's progress is only useful while it runs. The transcript rotates one generation back at 8 MB.

    Pick the interval by how fresh you need mail to be, not by how much work a pass does: every step is cursor-driven, so a quiet four-hour cadence costs about what four hourly passes cost, minus three wake-ups.

    The interval is measured, not assumed (2026-10-09). Onboarding installs the schedule itself and decides the cadence from the pass it just ran: the wall time of its own ingest work (the scan, the agent sessions, the archives) under thirty minutes earns the hourly schedule; longer earns the constrained setting, once a night at 03:00 local, because a pass that long is hours of the whole machine and a person on such a box is happy with any answer, not a real-time one. The decision and the measured time are printed on the schedule line (every 60 min - measured: the pass took 12 s (under 30 min earns hourly)) and recorded beside the store's transcript (~/.docenta/sync-schedule.json for the machine's store, <data dir>/logs/sync-schedule.json for any other). Every whole pass after that is a measurement too, and who ran it decides when the decision is applied: a by-hand docenta update that crosses the line in either direction re-registers the job at the cadence it earned and says so; a scheduled pass records its time (it runs under the very job it would reload) and the next docenta update, docenta schedule migrate or docenta setup update applies it; and the pass docenta setup update starts detached after a binary swap (docenta update --scheduled --after-swap, section 3.5) runs with the scheduler's posture but outside the job, so it records AND re-registers

    • that is how a box re-measures after a binary change, from a timed

    pass after the system had a chance to catch up, never from a stale record. A pass narrowed with --only or --stage measures nothing. docenta update --dry-run opens the store read-only (the state database query-only, no migration, no lock) and leaves its bytes as they were. A cadence you set yourself with schedule on --every or --daily-at is recorded as explicit and never moved by a measurement; the bare schedule on is the hourly default and may be. A machine asleep at 03:00 runs the pass when it wakes. Every registration runs at low priority (launchd Background with nice 10 and low-priority I/O, systemd Nice=10 with idle I/O scheduling, Task Scheduler priority 7), so the pass never fights the person for the keyboard. schedule status prints the cadence in words with the measurement it rests on (every 1 h (measured: last pass 12 s), or set by hand, never re-measured), the last pass's duration step by step, and a suggestion to go daily when a pass eats more than half its interval.

    Two hazards worth knowing about, both learned the hard way and both now handled by the command itself: scheduled jobs get a 256 file-descriptor limit that is too low for a recovery pass (each binary raises its own), and an ad-hoc-signed binary makes macOS re-prompt for privacy access on every pass (the pass reports it in the transcript instead of leaving you to wonder about the popups).

    7.3 Pausing without disabling anything#

    Before benchmarks, big migrations, or when you want the machine quiet:

    bash
    touch ~/.docenta/sync.pause     # pause: passes exit immediately
rm ~/.docenta/sync.pause        # resume

    The switch is just the presence of that file, so it survives reboots and needs no privileges. A second safeguard runs inside the pipeline itself: a lock file means two pipelines can never run at once, which is what once drove this machine into swap.

    7.4 Watching the build#

    bash
    docenta layers status

    The first lines name the runtime and the lane every model step will run on: runtime : onnxruntime 1.24.4-dml at ... - providers cpu, directml and lane : directml available. A lane line that says MISSING means the installed runtime has no provider for this platform's GPU lane and every step runs on the CPU; docenta setup update installs the channel's runtime for the platform. docenta setup runtime prints the same two lines on their own (--json for a tool).

    layer                           position        head    built
unit-index                     135101358   135101358   100.0%
dense:arctic-embed-m-v2.0      135101358   135101358   100.0%
mentions                       135101358   135101358   100.0%

    Add --watch to re-render every two seconds while you watch a long build. Your AI agent sees this same information through status, which is how it can honestly say "the semantic layer is 60 percent built" instead of pretending it has everything.

    Below the table, one rates line per model step says what this machine has achieved on it: dense:<model>: best 1,560/min on directml (2026-09-26), last 73/min on cpu (2026-10-05). The record (rates.json beside the cursors) keeps the best run per step, model and lane, and the most recent one; runs of fewer than 200 units or under a minute inside the model are not recorded. The rate is units over the time spent inside the model, not the wall clock, so a pass that mostly skips unchanged documents does not read as slow. Every embed and sparse pass compares itself against that best once it is past its warm-up (100 units and a minute inside the model): a run below one fifth of the machine's own best says so once, in the log and on the progress line (rate: 73 units/min is 1/21 of this box's 1,560 units/min on directml (recorded 2026-09-26)). That line was the missing one when a machine lost its GPU runtime and embedded on the cpu for a day while every step line still looked normal; the fix it points at is docenta setup verify and docenta setup update.

    8. Maintenance#

    Docenta is designed to need very little of this. Most upkeep happens by itself; this chapter is what to do when it does not.

    8.0 Space back in one command: docenta tidy (new)#

    Note

    New in the CLI arc's first phase (2026-10-09); the store's reclaim, gc, compact and expire verbs it replaces were retired in the third phase the same day (tidy --only gc|compact|semantic-compact|expire runs one piece alone). tidy is the same reclaim with two more steps and one flag; DOCENTA_ACCEPT_REMOVAL_WAVE=1 is still honoured for one release.

    docenta tidy is the reclaim as section 8.1 describes it - the reconcile walk of the roots the store owns, the content policy, gc, the semantic prune, the compaction, the semantic catch-up, the semantic compact - and then two things the door rebuilds of 2026-10-08 taught: the semantic stack runs ONCE MORE after the compaction (the pipeline to the feed head, so the run ends current by the pipeline's own word), and the final check prints every layer's state with the vectors each partition holds.

    The two breakers stay. gc refuses a pass that would collect an implausible share of the store (the mass-orphan limit: from 10,000 orphans at over 5 percent), and the semantic layers refuse a removal wave of the same shape. What your own exclusion rules retired is not weighed by either: a file that is still on disk but now excluded (a folder you set aside, a .gitignore, a path rule) is a decision you made, not a misclassification, so gc collects it whatever its share, records it beside the change feed, and the semantic layers remove it without counting it as a wave. Only files that are gone or replaced, and content no file names any more, are weighed. One flag is the reviewed acceptance of BOTH breakers for those:

    bash
    docenta tidy                       # the whole sequence; a wave stops it with the numbers
docenta tidy --force-wave          # you have checked the files are really gone (or really excluded): both breakers accept
docenta tidy --only gc             # one piece alone: gc | compact | semantic-compact | expire
docenta tidy --no-reconcile        # a store that names no roots
docenta tidy --repair              # decode-verify every frame first; the walk re-extracts

    --force-wave replaces the retired gc verb's --force and the environment variable DOCENTA_ACCEPT_REMOVAL_WAVE=1; the variable is still honoured for one release so a script written before this verb keeps working, and the run says so when it is the variable that accepted the wave. On the Intel Mac on 2026-10-09 the same outcome took the reclaim (gc refused), the forced gc, the reclaim again; it is one tidy --force-wave now.

    docenta update runs tidy as its third stage without the walk (the update's own scan just walked): when the compaction is due by the coverage threshold the reclaim runs, otherwise the semantic prune and the final check; always on an update you type, by threshold on a scheduled one.

    8.1 The commands, and when to reach for each#

    CommandRun it whenWhat it doesWhat it never touches
    docenta tidy --only compactRarely by hand - it runs automatically. After deleting a lot of content.Recompresses every sidecar at maximum compression into fresh packs, checkpoints and vacuums the database, force-merges the search index.Your files. Content is unchanged.
    docenta tidy --only gcAfter deleting many files from disk.Removes derivatives of files that no longer exist anywhere. Idempotent.Anything still referenced by a live path.
    docenta store verifyAny time you want proof. Monthly is plenty.Samples what it stored, compares it byte-for-byte against the files on disk, checks phrase-search accuracy, reports latency.Nothing - it is read-only.
    docenta store backup --to DIRBefore an update that migrates the schema, and on a schedule of your choosing.Copies the backup set while docenta runs: state.db and every license database by SQLite's online backup (a consistent snapshot even while the MCP server writes), the config and the license's other files, each database copy checked; then the blobs, incrementally, into a folder every backup under DIR shares. Writes DIR/<UTC stamp>/backup.json.Your files, and the live store: it only reads it.
    docenta store check [FILE]To prove a backup copy sound, or the live catalog.PRAGMA quick_check and PRAGMA foreign_key_check with docenta's path collation registered, read-only; exits non-zero when not sound.Anything - it is read-only.
    docenta update --only reindexOnly if the search index is lost or corrupted (the update runs it by itself when the index predates the build's schema).Rebuilds the index by replaying the publication log. Resumes if interrupted; docenta update --only reindex -- --fresh starts over.The database and sidecars (the index is a view of them).
    docenta tidy --only semantic-compactAfter a big first build ("seed").Folds the unit index's fragments and garbage-heavy segments, rewrites vector partitions, then rebuilds the dense query snapshot. A clean segment past a million live documents is left alone by design (rewriting it buys nothing); the report says how many were left and why, and names a merge that failed for lack of disk. --units --everything folds every segment into one regardless (a whole-index rewrite; the measured arm against the designed shape).The docenta store beneath it.
    docenta store reset --yesStarting over deliberately.Deletes every derived store: database, blobs, bundles, index, semantic layer, cursors.Your files, the models, the ONNX runtime, your config, and the logs.
    docenta layers resetChanging model or analyzer.Deletes only the semantic layer (--units or --vectors to scope it).The docenta store beneath it.
    docenta uninstall --list / docenta uninstall <part>... / docenta uninstall --everythingWalking back what onboarding did: one part, or all of it.--list shows what is on this machine: agents (the entries in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor), schedule (the hourly sync), mail (accounts, their secrets in the credential store with Google grants revoked, the mail spool), chats (the rendered AI sessions, exports and repository histories), stores (every store docenta built), license (device key, lease, seal), assets (models and runtime, about 3 GB to fetch again). <part> takes the named parts; --everything all of them in that order. A store goes on the hours its FIRST build cost, typed back, said as it happened, with the turbo GPU hours it burned of what this device was granted; a receipt of what went lands in your home directory. Add --page and the same plan is written as one local HTML file and opened in your browser, with room to explain it - the page never decides, the typed confirmation stays in the terminal and nothing listens on an address.Your files, mail and repositories, always. The binaries (see the next row).
    docenta uninstall binariesTaking the binaries off the machine, the inverse of the install line.The binaries in their folder, the app bundle on macOS, the channel record. Anything onboarding built is named and left alone; run docenta uninstall --everything first to take those too; at its end it names what is still on the machine (the logs of the passes, your settings file), which is yours to keep or delete.Everything onboarding built, unless removed first.

    docenta store reset --page writes the same plan as one local HTML file and opens it: what goes, what stays (your files, the models, the runtime, the config, the logs, each said plainly), what the first build cost and what a rebuild costs. The page never decides; the typed confirmation stays in the terminal and nothing listens on an address.

    Both reset commands print a plan with sizes and require a typed yes unless you pass --yes. docenta store reset also tells you how long your last full ingest took, so you know exactly what you are signing up to redo.

    8.2 Compaction happens by itself#

    Note

    You do not normally run docenta tidy --only compact. A successful ingest or scan checks how much of the store sits outside the last compaction and compacts when more than 20 percent (and at least 256 MB) is uncovered. A brand-new store is 100 percent uncovered, so your first ingest always ends with a compaction.

    Two things to know:

    • Skip it when you are in a hurry with --no-compact on ingest folder or
      • ingest machine. There is no other setting.
    • Compaction wants headroom. The index force-merge writes the merged
      • result before dropping the old segments, so it needs roughly the index's own size in free disk. If it cannot, it *skips safely* and tells you - your live data is never left in a partial state.

    There is one recorded open issue: on rare occasions an ingest-triggered compaction has spun for hours without writing. If you see that, kill it and re-run the ingest with --no-compact; nothing is damaged.

    8.3 What lives where, and how big it gets#

    bash
    docenta status --storage

    The machine every number below comes from, so you can hold your own up against it:

    Files on disk, as they sit there1.8 million files, 358 GB - counted the way your file manager counts them, copies and all
    Actually different things among them839,000 items, 125 GB - the rest are duplicates
    What is in it885,000 text and code files, 627,000 photos and images, 289,000 documents - including 255,000 emails going back to 2010 - plus video, audio, and years of AI chat transcripts
    Machinea MacBook Pro laptop (M4 Max, 16 cores, 64 GB memory) - not a server
    Disk docenta uses for all of it64 GB, 18 percent of the 358 GB it covers
    How fast a search isabout a twentieth of a second - faster than a blink. The slowest one in twenty takes about a quarter of a second; pulling up the passage itself is quicker still

    8.3.1 What each thing you add costs#

    Docenta is built up in pieces. You start by scanning the machine, and after that every source is something you add when you want it and skip when you do not. Each block below gives the same three answers for one source: how big it is, how much disk docenta spends on it, and how long each step takes.

    All figures are from the reference machine described above. Sizes are measured; the per-source disk and timings are those measurements applied to each source's own share.

    Note the pattern before you read them: the first build is fast per item because it processes in bulk, while later additions go through the change feed one item at a time. Adding a million things later costs more than having them there from the start - though "more" still means hours, not days.

    1. The machine's own files - where everyone starts#

    What it is1.48 million files, 308 GB, mostly code, documents, photos and video
    Disk docenta spends~53 GB
    docenta ingest machine1 hour 45 minutes - and this part is not optional

    That hour and three quarters is the whole scan side, and at the end of it you can already search every file by its contents.

    Everything after it is the semantic side, and it is four decisions, not one. They do not form a single chain: two of them branch off the first, and the last one does not need any of the others at all.

         docenta ingest machine  (1h45, required)
             |
  +----------+------------------------+
  |                                   |
  1. passage index  (30 min)      4. the people layer  (minutes)
  |                               entity cards, timelines, themes
  +--------------+
  |              |
  2. meaning-    3. code
  vectors        vectors
  (13 h)         (2 h)
    StepWhat you get for itTimeNeedsIf you skip it
    1. passage indexAnswers anchored to the exact paragraph instead of the whole file~30 minthe scanYou keep whole-file search; steps 2 and 3 become unavailable
    2. meaning-vectorsSearch by what you meant rather than what you typed~13 hoursstep 1The big one. You keep keyword, phrase and paragraph-level citations
    3. code vectorsCode search that understands symbols and definitions~2 hoursstep 1Only matters if you keep source code; keyword search on code still works
    4. the people layerEntity cards, timelines, and themesminutesthe scan onlyYou lose "everything about this person" and "what happened in 2019"

    Three things follow from that shape, and they are the whole decision:

    Steps 2 and 3 are independent of each other. Each builds its own separate set of vectors with its own bookmark, so you can have code search without general meaning search, or the other way round, or both. Neither needs the other.

    The people layer needs nothing but the scan. It reads the extracted text directly and never touches the passage index or the vectors. So "I want timelines but I am not paying thirteen hours for vectors" is not a compromise

    • it is a supported route, and it costs minutes.

    Step 2 does not have to be swallowed whole. It works through your material in order and writes down where it got to, so you can run it for an hour tonight and an hour tomorrow, and whatever it has finished already answers queries in the meantime - a partial build is not a broken one, just a smaller one. There is also --only-kind if you want to restrict it to particular kinds of content.

    Which models do this work, and can you choose?#

    Steps 2 and 3 are the only places docenta uses a model to build anything, and each step uses exactly one model. By default that is two models, run one after the other - the general one over everything you own, then the code specialist over your source code only. They are not run together; each takes the machine in turn, using all its cores while it does.

    You can substitute either one, and the trade is speed against how often the right answer comes back:

    ModelCoversSpeedTime on this collectionRight answer in the top ten
    the standard model - what you get by defaulteverything1,840 passages/min~12 hours70 percent
    a lighter alternativeeverything2,900 passages/min~8 hours44 percent
    the code specialist - the default for source codesource code only928 passages/min~2 hoursclearly ahead of any general model on code questions

    What "70 percent" actually means, because the number looks worse than it is. It is measured by asking 57 real questions - the kind you would actually ask, phrased the way you would actually phrase them - and checking whether the one document that answers each is in the top ten results, out of 839,000. The right document is the *first* result for about 37 percent of them.

    The honest comparison is not against some perfect score, it is against what you have today. Ordinary file search cannot answer these questions at all: it looks at names, so "which insurance letter mentioned the main-drain test" returns nothing unless you happened to put those words in a filename. Going from *cannot ask* to *right answer on the first page seven times in ten* is the whole product. Retrieval research measures itself in the same range on standard test sets; being right most of the time is what good looks like here, not a shortfall.

    Two cautions in the same breath, so the number is not oversold. Those 57 questions are our own, and we judged the answers ourselves - a small, self-graded exam, which is why we treat it as a floor to defend rather than a score to boast about. And it measures the *whole* system, keyword and meaning and all, which is the thing you actually use.

    Read the speed and accuracy columns together before reaching for the faster model. The lighter alternative saves about four hours once, and gets the right answer for 44 percent of questions instead of 70 - roughly a third fewer answers found, permanently, every day you use the system. Four hours is one evening; the accuracy is forever. Install the default and let it run overnight.

    How the code specialist finds your code - it does not read everything. It walks the same list as the other step but checks each entry's label first, and anything that is not a code declaration is dropped before any file is opened or any model runs. Skimming past a million non-code passages that way costs about eight minutes. Only actual declarations - functions, types, methods, about 123,000 of them here - go through the model, which is why the step is two hours rather than the day you would fear from its slower rate. If you keep no source code, it finds nothing and finishes almost immediately.

    There is no way to have several general models cover your material at once, and no reason to want it: they would each rebuild the same passages at their own cost, and searches read from one. Sets left behind by an earlier model choice are simply dead weight - see the note on unused models above.

    2. Adding an email archive - the best value in the system#

    What it is337,000 messages, 50 GB of mailbox, 20 years of it
    Disk docenta spends~2 GB
    Importing it5 to 10 minutes - a 32 GB mailbox became 246,000 separate messages in 4.5
    passage index~3 hours
    meaning-vectors~40 minutes
    people and timelines~3 minutes

    Twenty years of mail becomes individually searchable for two gigabytes. Mail is thousands of small things rather than a few big ones, so the *index* is the slow part here and the vectors are cheap - the opposite of your files. The entity layer pays off most on this material: every correspondent, resolved across address changes.

    3. Adding your AI chat history#

    What it is2,600 conversations, 90 MB
    Disk docenta spends~130 MB
    Importing itminutes
    passage index~2 minutes
    meaning-vectors~3 minutes
    people and timelinesseconds

    Effectively free. Every decision you reasoned through with an assistant becomes searchable evidence instead of something you half-remember.

    4. Adding your git history#

    What it is4,100 commits, 20 MB
    Disk docenta spends~30 MB
    Everything, all stepsunder 5 minutes

    Every repository in scope, every commit of every author on every branch: the message, both identities and dates, the parents, the refs, and every changed path with its line counts. Onboarding runs it as its git step and prints the repositories and the commit count of each; the pass renders the delta from then on. This is what makes "why did we change this, and when" a search (section 6.4).

    5. Adding messenger chats#

    What it isdepends entirely on your history; a WhatsApp export is typically hundreds of MB
    Disk docenta spendssmall - these are short text messages
    Everything, all stepsminutes for a typical export

    Not yet imported on the reference machine, so these are shapes rather than measurements.

    6. Reading the pictures you already have#

    What it isthe 223,000 images already scanned in step 1
    Disk docenta spends~0.5 GB
    Reading them~22 hours, in the background, stop and resume freely
    Making them searchable afterwardsabout a minute

    No new files - this reads what is already there. For most people it is the difference between scanned paperwork being findable or invisible.

    Adding it all up#

    DiskTime
    Machine files~53 GB~15 hours, of which 13 is the vectors
    Email archive~2 GB~4 hours
    AI chats, git, messengers~0.2 GBminutes
    Reading pictures~0.5 GB~22 hours in the background
    Models3 GBthe download

    Skip the meaning-vectors and the whole thing is a morning's work. Keep them and it is an overnight run you start once and never repeat - and from then on a normal day's changes go through every step in well under a minute, which is why the hourly sync is something you switch on and forget.

    Two things make the first build less imposing than the numbers suggest. You can search from the first minutes, while everything else is still building. And every step stops and resumes - close the laptop, kill it, lose power - because each one records how far it got.

    8.3.2 The three groups: what each part is for#

    Everything docenta writes falls into three groups, and the useful way to think about disk is to decide about the groups, not the individual files.

    Group 1: the engine - finding words in your files#

    27 GB, 7.5 percent of what it covers.

    This is docenta itself; if you use it at all, you have this. It needs no models and no AI runtime: plain extraction and indexing.

    It walks roughly 850,000 files and 270 GB per hour, and that covers far more material than the finished size suggests, because most of what any real machine holds is copies. The 1.8 million files on this one contain only 839,000 different things: two and a half copies of each on average. The same attachment sits in four mailboxes, the same document in a backup and a working folder, the same photo across three exports. Every copy is still read - identity comes from content, not from the filename, so there is no way to know something is a copy without reading it - but each distinct thing is extracted and indexed exactly once.

    That is the main reason docenta is quick on a real machine, and why its footprint tracks what you actually *have* rather than how many places you happen to keep it.

    Re-scans afterwards are a different order of magnitude again: 2.5 million files re-checked in five minutes, because a file whose size and timestamp have not changed is skipped without being opened at all.

    PartSizeIn plain words
    the search index11.7 GBThe index at the back of a book, for every word in every file: which documents contain it. This is what makes a search instant instead of a grep.
    the extracted text11.5 GBA compressed, readable copy of the words found inside your PDFs, Office files, and mail. It is what search results quote, and what lets you read a passage without opening the original.
    the content map2.8 GBWhich content lives at which paths, what has been seen, what changed. Docenta's memory of your filesystem.
    the change feed1.0 GBA running list of what was extracted and when: the queue the meaning layers read from.

    Can you skip parts of it? No. These four work as one thing, and together they are the complete product: keyword, phrase, and regex search across everything, with exact citations. Many people never need more than this.

    Group 2: the meaning layer - what you can pick and choose#

    33 GB of representation plus about 3 GB of models. This is where the real choices are, because it is not one thing: it is two independent branches that both sit on group 1, and you can take either, both, or neither.

                   GROUP 1: the core                27 GB   7.5%   2-3 h
               files, extracted text, index     no models needed
                           |
           +---------------+----------------+
           |                                |
     BRANCH A: meaning                BRANCH B: the graph
           |                                |
  passage index  27.5 GB  7.7%   ~30 min    mentions   ..
           |                                entities   ..  0.4 GB
  meaning-vectors 4.7 GB  1.3%   ~12 h      gazetteer  ..  0.1%
                                            claims     ..  minutes
                                            communities..  no models

    The two branches do not depend on each other. The graph layers read the extracted text from group 1 directly; they never touch the passage index or the vectors. So the case of wanting people and timelines but not vectorization works exactly as you would hope - and it is the cheapest thing in the system.

    Branch A: search by meaning

    StepWhat it gives youSpaceShareTime to buildNeeds
    passage indexAnswers that point at the exact paragraph rather than the file. Also the substrate everything else in this branch stands on.27.5 GB7.7%tens of minutesgroup 1
    meaning-vectorsFinds a document that never used your words - "the plumber who fixed the main drain" reaching a letter that says neither.4.7 GB1.3%12 hoursthe passage index

    Branch B: people, timelines, and themes

    StepWhat it gives youNeeds
    mentionsEvery name, company, address, and account found in the text.group 1
    entitiesThose mentions resolved into actual people and organisations.mentions
    gazetteerSpelling variants and alternative names bound to the right entity.entities
    claimsDated statements, which is what a timeline is assembled from.entities
    communitiesThemes: clusters of entities that keep appearing together.claims

    The whole branch is 0.4 GB, about 0.1 percent of the corpus, and minutes of work - on the reference machine a pass over 34,500 new documents took 18 seconds across all five steps. It needs no models at all. Each step does depend on the one above it, but since the whole chain costs minutes there is no practical reason to stop part way; one command runs all five.

    The asymmetry worth staring at

    SpaceTime
    passage index27.5 GB (83% of group 2)tens of minutes
    meaning-vectors4.7 GB (14%)12 hours (95% of the time)
    the whole graph0.4 GB (1%)minutes

    The vectors cost almost nothing in space and almost all of the time. The passage index is the reverse. The graph is nearly free on both axes. So the decision is not "how much disk do I have" but which of the three you actually want, and they price very differently.

    So, concretely:

    • Want everything? Run docenta layers pipeline. Budget half a day for
      • the first pass, mostly the vectors, and let it run overnight.
    • Want precise citations and people and timelines, but not meaning-search?
      • Run docenta layers pipeline --only index, then --only sparse, --only mentions, --only entities, --only gazetteer, claims, communities. You save 12 hours and 4.7 GB, and you skip the embedding models entirely.
    • Want only people and timelines? Run just the five graph steps. 0.4 GB,
      • a few minutes, no models, no GPU, no ONNX runtime. This is the single best value in docenta and most people do not realise it is available on its own.
    • Want none of it? Do not run the second binary at all. Group 1 alone is a
      • complete citing keyword system.

    The timings above are from an M4 with the embedding running on CPU. A machine with a usable GPU lane, or a smaller corpus, will move the 12-hour figure the most - it is the one number here that is hardware-bound rather than corpus-bound.

    Group 3: reading pictures - OCR#

    Under 1 GB of disk, and about 22 hours of background work for the 223,000 images on this machine - a measured 10,000 images per hour. It runs beside everything else and can be stopped and resumed at will, so it costs you waiting time only if you choose to wait. Optional, and very cheap in space.

    PartSizeIn plain words
    analysis bundles0.5 GBThe text read out of scanned documents and photographs, stored beside the image it came from.
    OCR models0.2 GBThe two small models that do the reading.
