    Can you skip it? Yes - the update skips the step on a machine without the OCR models. You lose the ability to search the contents of scans, faxes, and photographed documents; everything else is unaffected. For most people this is the best value per gigabyte in the whole system, because scanned paperwork is exactly the material that is otherwise impossible to find.

    The models#

    About 3 GB for a working installation, and this cost does not grow with your corpus - it is the same whether you index 10 GB or 10 TB.

    ItemSizeNeeded for
    arctic-embed-m-v2.0 - the embedder1.2 GBmeaning-based search (group 2)
    sparse-doc-v3-distill - the sparse encoder0.35 GBthe strongest ranking channel (group 2)
    bge-reranker-base - the reranker1.1 GBputting the best few answers in order
    The ONNX Runtimeunder 0.1 GBrunning all three on your own chips

    These are the measured sizes on disk of what onboarding fetches. docenta setup verify lists each one and says whether it is present.

    The ratio that matters: your files, and docenta's representation of them.

    The reference machine has about 800 GB of data on its disk. Docenta covers 1.8 million files holding 358 GB of raw bytes - the rest is skipped by the default hygiene rules (build trees, package caches, system files) or is cloud material with no local bytes. Those 358 GB cost 64 GB, all in:

    The corpus358 GB of files, 1.8 million of them
    Group 1, the engine27 GB
    Group 2, the meaning layer33 GB
    Group 3, reading pictures0.7 GB
    The models3 GB
    Total on disk64 GB, about 18 percent of the corpus

    So a searchable, citable, meaning-aware representation of a third of a terabyte of files costs 18 percent of what those files themselves occupy. If disk is tight, group 1 alone is 7.5 percent - and it needs no models and no AI runtime at all, just the engine. A complete keyword, phrase, and regex search system over everything you own, with exact citations, for a fourteenth of what the files themselves take.

    Your ratio will differ, and the reason is simple: only text becomes an index. A photo or video library is recorded from its metadata and costs almost nothing, so a media-heavy machine lands in the low single digits. A corpus of source code, documents, and mail is nearly all text and can reach 40 to 50 percent. The mix on this machine - code, documents, images, mail, and media together - is what produces 18 percent.

    One more thing worth planning around: a first semantic build is temporarily much larger than its settled size, which is why docenta tidy --only semantic-compact after a big first pass is worth running. Compaction generally reclaims 25 to 45 percent of the pre-compaction total.

    Everything lives under one data root, which docenta setup config will print. You can relocate any store by uncommenting the matching key in config.toml; the guidance in that file says which ones want your fastest disk (the index, the bundles, and the state database are the IO-hot ones). Models are the exception: they take an absolute path and move with docenta setup models --move, which copies, verifies every digest, and only then deletes the source.

    8.4 Backups#

    The honest answer: back up your files, not docenta. Every byte docenta stores is derived and can be rebuilt by re-ingesting. If you want to avoid the rebuild time, stop all docenta processes and copy the whole data root as a unit - copying it while a scan runs will give you an inconsistent snapshot.

    The two things that are *not* rebuildable and deserve a copy: your config.toml, and ~/.docenta/spool-state/imap.toml if you set up mail.

    Big documents are read in windows, never held whole, so a multi-gigabyte text, CSV or JSON file costs the same memory as a small one. What it costs instead is index space, and only when the content is worth indexing: a machine-generated body (a log, a minified bundle, generated code) is stored and fetchable in full but gets no search postings.

    Size limits, and what they mean: a document a person wrote to be read (text, markdown, Org, JSON, CSV, XML, YAML, HTML, RTF, Office including the macro-enabled kinds, PDF, EPUB, notebooks, mail files and source code; the list is [limits] whole_document_extensions) is ingested whole at any size. A machine-generated file (a log, a trace, a dump, a line-delimited stream, an unknown extension) is recorded metadata-only over max_extract_bytes (256 MiB) and its text is cut at max_body_text_chars. When the text you are served is such a cut, the hit and the fetch say extraction_truncated: true: what you read is real, the tail is not held.

    Every bound a lane keeps, stated (the audit of 2026-10-09, docs/architecture/ingestion-coverage-audit-2026-10-09.md, holds the reasoning row by row; nothing else limits what is ingested, and a filter that was someone's guess is gone or listed there as open work):

    lanethe boundvaluekeywhat refuses
    the walknone by extension: every regular file the policy admits is walked and recorded; a file no lane reads waits for one with the reason on its row (docenta status --waiting unknown)---ext, --family narrow a folder's walknothing is dropped; what no lane reads is listed as waiting
    the enginethe sniff: a file of an extension no lane reads (or none) is read once for text within this bound1 MiB[limits] sniff_max_bytesover it the row waits with the bound as its reason; the finish step reads it when the bound grows
    the walkthe hygiene set and the OS treesthe lists in [discovery] excludes[discovery] excludes, .docentaignorecaches, build output, package trees, app bundles, editor stores, cloud mounts
    the walk.gitignore chainson[discovery] respect_gitignore; [discovery] includes or a !pattern crumb admit past itwhat git ignores, each a recorded ignored gap in status --waiting
    the enginethe largest file hashed whole512 MiB[limits] max_full_hash_bytesmetadata-only above it
    the enginethe largest non-whole file read256 MiB[limits] max_extract_bytesmetadata-only above it; the whole-document list is exempt
    the enginethe longest non-whole body256 Mi chars[limits] max_body_text_chars (0 = off)the tail, said as extraction_truncated
    the engineone file's extraction60 s + 1 s per MiB, 4 GiB[limits] extract_timeout_secs, extract_memory_bytesthe file fails and is retried
    the enginechildren of children3 generations (a scan in a message forwarded in a message)[limits] max_child_deptha child past it is a recorded bound gap in status --waiting; a raised key delivers it at the parent's next extraction
    the text lanethe largest non-whole text64 MiB[limits] max_plain_text_bytesmetadata-only above it
    the document lanethe largest non-whole document (a template, a show, a walked mbox)256 MiB[limits] max_document_bytesmetadata-only above it, re-read by the finish step when the bound grows; the whole-document list is exempt
    the image lanethe largest decode100 MP[limits] max_image_pixelsthe perceptual hash; the metadata stays
    the archive laneone archive, one member, the decompressed output of one archive, members as children256 MiB, 32 MiB, 512 MiB, no count bound[limits] archive_max_bytes, archive_member_max_bytes, archive_max_out_bytes, archive_max_members (0 = none)every member not delivered stays listed and is a recorded gap (bound, or encrypted) in status --waiting
    the document lanethe pictures inside a docx, pptx, xlsx, ODF file or EPUB, delivered as children512 MiB of decompressed pictures per document[limits] archive_max_out_bytesa picture past it is a recorded gap naming the key
    the walkarchives the walk finds (not attachments)listed, not exploded[limits] walked_archives = "explode", or a walk with --family archive / --ext zipthe members wait as one recorded gap per archive; attachments always explode
    mail archivesone message of an mbox256 MiB[discovery] max_file_bytesthe message keeps its row, loses its text; 2 GiB of messages in flight at most
    mail (IMAP)one pass200 messages, drained until currentbatch in imap.tomlnothing: the drain continues
    chatsthe facets block40 paths, 20 commands, 10 errors, 20 tests, 12 commits-the transcript holds the rest ([chats] transcript = full keeps everything)
    gitnone--every repository, every commit, every ref, the whole message
    OCRone hourly pass2000 documents or 45 min-the rest waits for the next pass
    semanticthe embed window512 tokens of 4,096 chars per input (8 chars a token), tail windows stepping by it, 128 per unit; every shipped model reads 512, measured against 1,024 and 2,048 (arctic lost, qwen unchanged)window_tokens in the model's manifest.json (a change re-embeds in place)the text past the last window has no vector; the lexical index has it whole
    semanticwhich files get tail windowsprose, code, property lists, XML and extensionless text; CSV, JSON, logs, svg, css, yaml, toml, conf, cfg and jsonl keep their first input (measured, the audit's S4)-the tail of those files is keyword-searchable, not meaning-searchable
    both indexesthe longest token indexed256 characters-a longer run of letters and digits (an encoded blob, a minified string) is not a term; every hash, token and identifier a person types is

    One more key in config.toml worth knowing: [chats] transcript. Agent sessions (Claude Code, Codex) render as prose by default, the conversation plus a compact facets block folded from the tool traffic (files touched, commands, errors, tests, commits). Set it to full and nothing the agent did is thrown away: its reasoning, every tool call field by field, every tool result whole, each searchable as its own turn. A tool result Claude Code offloaded to a file beside the session (the transcript keeps a short preview) is read from that file, whole; the transcript of every agent a session spawned is a session of its own, with the session that spawned it and the task it was given named at the top. Sessions grow three to twenty times; the next hourly pass or docenta ingest claude re-renders every session in the new mode. A session over about 3 million characters is written in parts (<id>.eml, <id>.part2.eml and so on, one thread). Credentials an agent met on the way (a password in a config it read, a token in a command) are replaced by [redacted secret] before the session is written; the field name stays, so the line is still findable. This happens to AI sessions only: every other file is searchable exactly as you can read it.

    9. Upgrading#

    9.1 The normal upgrade#

    bash
    docenta setup update

    One command, nothing typed before or after it (section 3.5 lists its six steps: the sync held, the swap, the assets, the checks, the scheduled jobs migrated, the agent configs). It fetches the newest build when there is one, verifies it against the signed checksum list exactly as the first install did, and replaces every binary in ~/.docenta/bin (on Windows, %LOCALAPPDATA%\docenta\bin). When you are already current it says so and changes nothing. The handbook and the other documents in ~/.docenta/doc are replaced with the build, so the book you open always matches the programs you run.

    Each file is written under a temporary name beside the binaries and then renamed into place, so replacing a running binary is safe: anything looking at the file sees the whole old one or the whole new one, never half of each. The staging directory sits beside the binaries on purpose: a temp directory on another filesystem (systemd's private temp, a tmpfs) cannot be renamed across, and the updater copies where a rename cannot.

    Warning

    Never copy a binary over a running one by hand. On macOS that invalidates its signature and the program dies silently at its next launch. The update command is the only thing that should touch that folder.

    9.2 Your agent does not need restarting#

    docenta serve runs as a supervisor that watches its own binary on disk. When you install a new version, it starts a fresh worker, replays the handshake, and hands over between requests - with no visible downtime and no config change: the hub of the old build leaves once no call is in flight, and each session's own docenta serve shim re-attaches on the next line, the first one starting a hub of the new build. Your agent keeps its session, and is sent notifications/tools/list_changed so that it lists the tools again: a session that has been idle for days hears of the new build too, because its shim watches the binary while the hub has it dropped for silence and nudges it the moment the binary changes. Whether the agent acts on the nudge is the client's doing; status names the serving generation in tool_names either way.

    9.3 The database migrates itself#

    Schema changes apply automatically the next time any write command runs. You can also do it explicitly:

    bash
    docenta store init

    which reports already at schema revision N or the from/to pair. Migrations run one transaction each and roll back on failure, so an interrupted upgrade leaves the database at its last consistent revision.

    9.4 Do you need to re-ingest? Almost never#

    Docenta keys every stored extraction by a recipe: the content, the lane, its version, and the schema. When an upgrade improves an extractor, the recipe changes, and the next walk over those files re-extracts them automatically rather than hiding behind an unchanged timestamp. To refresh one modality deliberately:

    bash
    docenta ingest folder ~/Documents --family document

    The exceptions, all of which announce themselves:

    • docenta update --only backfill - only for stores created before the change
      • feed existed. It synthesizes the missing feed entries from data already on disk without re-reading a single source file.
    • docenta update --only analysis - after the OCR producer has run. A bundle
      • landing beside unchanged bytes is invisible to a normal walk, so this republishes exactly those.
    • docenta layers reset --vectors --yes, then layers pipeline --only embed - after changing
      • the embedding model.
    • Nothing - after a change to which files get tail windows (the extra embed inputs that
      • cover a long passage past its first 4,096 characters). The embed step notices a partition built under an older rule and walks the store for the missing windows itself, in the hourly pass's own time slices, and docenta layers status shows one tail windows line per partition: current, walking N of M, or owed. The walk can also be run by hand (docenta dev embed --tail-windows, with --model-dir and --only-kind for a specialist partition); a partition seeded by the current build needs none, and a partition the store does not hold (a prose-only store has no code units, so the code model never wrote a vector) has nothing to walk: the step says so in one line and goes on, while the manual verb refuses a partition that is not there.
    • Nothing - after a model's embed window changes (the tokens of one input it is fed, the
      • window_tokens of its manifest.json; the inputs and the tail windows are sized by it, 8 characters a token). The partition keeps its name (the window is policy, not the model's identity) and its record says which window built it, so docenta layers status shows embed window: ... built at 512 tokens, the model reads 1024: a re-embed is owed, and the next embed pass under the lane word re-embeds the store in place in its own time slices (re-embedding, N of M); the partition answers searches all along. The Apple GPU variant is pinned at 512 tokens: a model whose window is wider embeds on the cpu and says why.
    • docenta layers reset --units --yes, then layers pipeline --only index, then
      • layers pipeline --only sparse - after an analyzer or schema change to the unit index. The index step builds the lexical index and attaches the sparse terms the cache already holds; a unit the cache lacks is indexed bare and counted. The sparse step encodes the bare units (--sparse local | turbo | later decides; later leaves the index in place and the step waiting) and upserts them; nothing bare means nothing to do.

    9.5 The runtime and its lanes#

    The ONNX runtime is an asset like the models, and it is the one asset whose contents decide whether your GPU is used at all: Microsoft builds it per platform with different execution providers inside, and a build without this platform's provider runs every model step on the CPU, ten to twenty times slower, with nothing visibly wrong. On 2026-10-05 the owner's Windows box did exactly that for a day after a runtime bump had moved it to Microsoft's CPU build (there is no DirectML build past 1.24.4). Four things now stand between that and you:

    1. The publisher declares the providers each platform's runtime must
      2. carry and inspects every archive before it is published; a runtime without its lane is not published.
    2. The channel's index carries that declaration, and docenta-setup
      3. (install, update, verify) asks the installed runtime what it carries - the runtime itself, not the file name - and names a gap: runtime : onnxruntime 1.28.0 lacks directml (the channel declares cpu, directml; the platform's lane directml is MISSING ...). A gap fails verify.
    3. A model step that asks for a lane the runtime lacks loads on the
      4. CPU in the CPU's full shape (every core, the CPU's batch budget), and its arming line says so: accel directml (auto) - fell back to cpu: the loaded ONNX Runtime has no directml provider. A lane that fell back is never compared against the CPU as if it were a GPU, so no parity verdict is cached for it.
    4. Every embed and sparse step records the rate it achieved on this box
      5. per model and lane, and a run far below the box's own best says so in its first minutes and in status (section 7.4).
    5. Every bulk lane runs its model in its own docenta-model-worker
      6. process (the dense models, the code model, the sparse encoder): the pipeline arms the lane by spawning the worker beside its own binary, drives it over the worker protocol, and drops it when the lane ends, so the lane's sessions - the runtime's arenas, a CoreML context and its graphics memory - go back to the OS before the next lane starts. Before 2026-10-16 the lanes ran in the one pipeline process and the finished lanes' sessions stayed resident: a 48 GB Mac carried 10 GB of graphics memory from the dense and sparse lanes while the code lane ran on the CPU, with the swap file full. The worker is recycled every 256 batches, so a runtime leak never accumulates across a long seed either; a worker that cannot arm its lane says why in the handshake, and the auto fallback to the CPU reads that reason the way it read the in-process load's.

    The Windows runtime stays at 1.24.4 with DirectML until Microsoft ships a DirectML build again or docenta grows a Windows ML lane; the pinned ort crate loads any runtime from 1.17 on, so the runtime version is the publisher's choice per platform, not the crate's.

    10. Troubleshooting#

    "Too many open files"#

    The scheduler's default file-descriptor limit is far too low for a recovery pass. Both binaries now raise their own limit at startup, and the sync script sets ulimit -n 8192. If you run passes from a custom wrapper, do the same.

    The machine is swapping, everything is slow#

    Almost always two pipelines running at once. The pipeline takes a lock (pipeline.lock in the semantic directory) and a second instance now exits immediately with another pipeline is already running on this store.

    Note

    If a pipeline was hard-killed on Windows the lock can linger: delete pipeline.lock and re-run.

    Also check whether a build tree or another job is eating the disk: docenta status --storage shows docenta's own footprint, and if that looks normal, the space is going somewhere else.

    "the semantic engine is not wired on this server"#

    Your agent is asking for meaning-based search before the layer exists. All three of these must be true: <semantic>/units exists, <semantic>/vectors exists, and your embedding model's manifest.json exists. Run docenta layers pipeline. The server re-checks on every call, so it starts working without a restart.

    "the semantic entity store is not built on this corpus yet"#

    Same idea for who_is, timeline, themes, and evidence: run docenta layers pipeline and they mount themselves.

    "loading ONNX Runtime from ...: ..."#

    The runtime is missing or somewhere unexpected. Run docenta setup update, which fetches it if it is absent and says where it put it, or set ORT_DYLIB_PATH to the full path of the library file.

    Search quality feels poor#

    Check which embedder actually armed. Run docenta layers pipeline --only embed -v and read the armed: line it prints - it names the model directory in use. If it says multilingual-e5-small or baseline Mix (no models installed), the production embedder is not installed: revisit chapter 3.4. This is the single most common quality problem, and it is silent by design (docenta prefers degrading to failing).

    Files exist but are not searchable#

    Run through these in order:

    1. docenta search "<something exact>" --json - is the file even in the
      2. corpus?
    2. Is it a cloud placeholder? Files stored only in iCloud, Google Drive,
      3. or OneDrive have no bytes locally. Docenta records them without reading them (which would trigger a full download of your entire cloud drive) and docenta store verify counts them as skips. A file already recorded this way is settled, so a walk never reads it again on its own: docenta update --only finish -- --fetch-from <folder> (the finish step with its folder) fetches and reads the placeholders under that folder, if you truly want the download.
    3. Is it a large mailbox? Mail containers over 256 MB are not exploded
      4. automatically; the ingest prints a note and waits for docenta ingest mailbox.
    4. Is it an archive other than ZIP? tar, 7z, and rar are cataloged
      5. but not expanded.
    5. Is it in an excluded directory? node_modules, target, .git,
      6. Library/CloudStorage and about forty other patterns are excluded by default for hygiene. docenta setup config shows your effective settings.
    6. Is it in another person's home directory? On a shared machine those
      7. are skipped by default, even where the permissions would allow reading them - someone else's account is not part of your material. Shared folders and shared volumes are still indexed, because those were shared deliberately. If you genuinely need one, name it: docenta ingest folder /Users/them/Projects still works.

    A long run looks hung#

    Use -v and watch the heartbeats, or docenta layers status --watch in another terminal. Two field lessons worth repeating: watch the binary's process and the cursor file, not a wrapper script's memory, and never run bulk passes with a debug build - one measured 150 times slower than release while looking perfectly healthy.

    Verify reports divergences#

    docenta store verify exits non-zero when stored text no longer matches disk or a sampled object fails its search probe. Run it with --json to see which content ids diverged. The search line reads hit / buried / miss: a probe is a phrase from the middle of the sampled object, and on a corpus with thousands of near-identical files (unpacked tarballs, stock-quote CSVs) the sampled one can sit below the probe depth. Verify then asks the same phrase of that object alone; a match is reported as buried (indexed and searchable, merely outranked - not an error), no match is a real miss. Ordinary causes: the file was edited after indexing (re-ingest fixes it) or it is a cloud placeholder (expected). If sidecar references point at pack files that no longer exist, docenta tidy --only compact --repair deletes those rows and marks the files for re-extraction on the next full scan.

    11. Command reference#

    docenta - the engine#

    The tree: four daily verbs at the top, everything else a verb under a noun (docenta <noun> --help lists the verbs).

    The daily verbs

    CommandPurpose
    search QUERYKeyword, phrase, regex, or literal search.
    read REFERENCEA window of a document's text, by content id, passage id or path (the MCP tool of the same name). related lists what sits beside it, thread the conversation a message belongs to.
    ask QUERYOne evidence pack (the semantic sibling's hidden answer verb beside it).
    shopThe shop: everything docenta sells, for this machine, on one page in the browser - Pro for one, two or three years ($95 / $180 / $245, rights, five GPU-hours of credit a year, paid once, no renewal by itself), packs of whole GPU-hours (5, 10, 25, 50), more seats on a Pro license (three come with it, six at most: $25 a seat for the remaining term, $45 once on a lifetime Pro), a grant code. A paid Pro is installed here, paid hours are credited here, paid seats are on the license at once; a machine with Pro for life sees no Pro term (nothing to buy) and a Pro code redeemed on it is refused unspent; the terminal waits for the site's word.
    license [status [--json] [--explain]]Pro's door: the license state of this machine (what it may do, the trial, the dates, the device key), then the same shop page with Pro first (with the hours first on a machine that has Pro for life: there is no term to buy for it, the page offers seats and packs); license status is the state alone (the report setup license gives).
    license devicesThe seats of this machine's license from this machine: every device bound to it by its device code, keystore and last renewal, live or idle (an idle seat - no renewal for longer than a lease lives - goes to the next device that binds). Runs docenta-license devices.
    license request [--out FILE]A license by file, step one, for a machine that must not talk: this machine's signed request file (its device key and nothing else; default docenta-license-request.bin here), to upload at license.docenta.ai/license.html from any browser or send to the operator. Runs docenta-license request --out FILE.
    license install FILEA license by file, step two: the lease file the license page (or the operator) handed back for THIS device, verified against the built-in root and kept; no network. Runs docenta-license install FILE --bundle.
    license release CODEGive a seat back: the device named by its code (license devices lists them), this machine's own included (its lease then runs out into the floor). The service records the release and mails the address on the license. Runs docenta-license release CODE.
    license rekeyMove this machine's device key into its hardware keystore (the Secure Enclave through the Docenta.app helper on a Mac, the TPM on Windows, a TPM 2.0 on Linux when this account can open /dev/tpmrm0, see "On Linux the device key" above): a key is made there, the license service binds the license to it, the lease is installed, the software key's public half is set aside as *.previous and its private key shredded. Runs docenta-license rekey --hardware. A Mac or a Windows machine on a software key while a hardware keystore is reachable is told so in steps (a Linux machine is offered the move and not pressed): a hint once, a daily reminder from day three (agents see it in their status), every run from day seven, the Pro acts held from day fourteen. With --lost the key is gone (a TPM clear, a restore to a new disk): a new one is made and the license moves to it, proven by the installed lease (the licenser's plain rekey).
    license activate [--token TOKEN]Bind this machine to a license: the code a purchase or a grant gave, or an operator's token. The shop does this for you; the verb is for a machine set up by hand. Runs the licenser's activate.
    license renew [--if-due]Renew the lease now; with --if-due only when it has less than a day left, which is what the renewal job runs every six hours. Runs the licenser's renew.
    license schedule install|status|heal|removeThe renewal job on this machine's own scheduler: register it, show it, register it again when the program it names has moved (an update does this by itself), remove it. Runs the licenser's schedule.
    license show [--last-exchange]The installed lease as it is; --last-exchange prints the last renewal request and answer byte for byte. Runs the licenser's show.
    license fingerprintThis machine's device key and its code; the key is made when there is none. Runs the licenser's fingerprint.
    license removeTake the lease off this machine: it is Free docenta from that moment; the device key and the seal stay. Runs the licenser's remove.
    serve [--read-only] [--profile NAME] [--page-budget CHARS]Serve the MCP tools to an agent over stdio. --read-only serves the reading tools only. --profile NAME is the serving profile of this registration's calls that name none (memory for a second registration docenta-memory), and --page-budget CHARS (8192 to 500000) the size a memory page may take on a host that accepts more than the default; a call's own profile or page_budget wins. All three are that session's own: every session of a store shares one hub and one brain.

    ingest - bringing content in

    CommandPurpose
    ingest folder DIR [--trust-folders]Index one directory tree. --trust-folders is for a corpus that does not change: the files of a folder are passed over when the folder's own modification time has not moved since a walk entered it and the store holds every file in it, so a re-walk costs one directory read per folder and an interrupted walk resumes where it stopped. A file rewritten in place is not seen; run without the switch after such an edit.
    ingest machineIndex every fixed drive, each with its own cursor.
    ingest manifest FILEProcess a work list written by dev enumerate.
    ingest mailbox FILEExplode one large mail container explicitly.
    ingest chatgpt ZIPA ChatGPT export, unzipped, rendered, ingested.
    ingest claude-ai MANIFESTA Claude account export: its parts fetched through your browser, rendered, ingested.
    ingest whatsappWhatsApp export drops.
    ingest claudeClaude Code sessions, now.
    ingest codexCodex sessions (~/.codex/sessions, the archive, the hook's copies; a copy and its live rollout render once, the longest of them), now.
    ingest zedZed's agent threads (its threads/threads.db, read from a copy so a running Zed is never locked; each thread one document with its title and project folder, the tool calls and results in the full transcript mode), now.
    [chats] transcript = 'full' (config)Agent sessions keep everything: reasoning, every tool call, every tool result. Default prose keeps the conversation plus the compact facets.
    ingest gitEvery repository's history as correspondence (every commit of every author on every ref, the delta after the first pass); --root DIR names the tree, --store NAME renders into that store's own spool.
    ingest ocr add|remove|list PATH...Tag files or folders for the next OCR sweep, drop the tags, show them.

    The source map - every source, its mode, its state, the command that advances it - is docenta status --sources. What used to be an ingest verb and is a STEP of docenta update since the verb map (2026-10-09):

    Step (update --only STEP)PurposeSwitches (after --)
    recoverReturn to what discovery could not examine: folders that would not list and paths that would not stat, retried on their own schedule, each ending as examined, absent, refused or orphaned. A change record the Windows journal could not place (a resolve row: the record's parent folder resolved to nothing by id) is returned to by what the record says: its own reference while the file still opens by id, then its name under the volume's roots within a per-run bound of 200,000 directory entries; a name found nowhere climbs the backoff ladder and after its passes ends as unresolvable, with the reason. A refusal (an admit gap: a path a .gitignore hid, a child or an archive member past a bound) is looked at and left pending while it stands, never climbed, and walked once the config admits it or the bound grows. docenta status --waiting lists what is pending, beside the files waiting on a lane.--limit N (places per run, default 200)
    finishRead the files an earlier run recorded without their text, for a reason that no longer holds: over a size limit today's settings lift. Such a file is settled, so no walk revisits it on its own; the step asks the exclusion policy for each and says what it left and why. A cloud placeholder is never downloaded by the update; docenta update --only finish -- --fetch-from DIR fetches one folder's placeholders by name and then runs the OCR over that folder's scans and images.--fetch-from DIR (repeatable)
    staleThe recipe sweep: re-extract the files a lane would now read differently, and no others (the update runs it once per build). The sweep of what came out empty is the step's own switch: docenta update --only stale -- --sparse-text; the plan alone is docenta update --dry-run.--sparse-text
    analysisRepublish content whose OCR bundle arrived.
    enrichBring an existing store up to the full capture without re-ingesting it (--missing rows only, which the update runs); docenta update --only enrich -- --fresh starts every pass over, -- --only PASS runs one (verdicts, labels, truncations, attachments, ...).--fresh, --only PASS
    backfillSynthesize feed entries for a pre-feed store (the update runs it only on a store that predates the change feed).
    promote-bodiesJudge the archived bodies again under this build's body-index policy (once per build; docenta update --dry-run counts what it would promote).
    reindexRebuild the search index from the publication log (the update runs it when the index predates the build's schema; docenta update --only reindex -- --fresh starts from an empty index). Allowed on a sealed store, like backfill and promote-bodies: update --only reindex on a door's store runs.--fresh
    expireEnd the absence hold (every update; tidy --only expire [--hold-days N] by hand).--hold-days N, --force

    A step's own switches ride on the update (2026-10-09): everything after -- goes to the one step --only names, so docenta update --only finish -- --fetch-from ~/Documents/scans is the finish step with its folder, and docenta update --only stale -- --sparse-text the stale step's empty-text sweep. Naming two steps, or none, with switches after -- is refused in one line. Every step is its own process under the update's runner (for the transcript, the timing, the receipt and the crash isolation); the entry it spawns is internal, like the extract worker, and nothing a person types.

    docenta update --dry-run is the whole pass's dry run: it prints the plan (the same read-only plan docenta status shows as "next update", stage by stage, what runs and what is skipped and why) and every planned step that has a dry run of its own runs it - stale says which files are behind, finish which recorded files it would read, promote-bodies how many bodies it would promote - and nothing is written: no transcript line, no receipt, no done marker, no summary of a pass that did not happen. --only STEP --dry-run narrows it to one step's dry run.

    sync - keeping it fresh

    CommandPurpose
    status [--content [--by-drive]|--storage|--pack [DIR]|--semantic|--sources|--waiting [FAMILY] [--limit N]|--progress|--runtime] [--json]One page: store, layers with the vectors held, the pending set, the consent, the sync, what the next update would do by stage; each flag opens the fuller page of the old verb. New (CLI arc phase 1); section 7.0.1.
    update [--only STEP]... [--stage ingest|semantic|tidy] [--scheduled] [--dry-run] [-v] [-- SWITCH...]The three stages in one pass, from the answers given; holds this store's schedule while it runs; quiet with a summary, -v streams. --dry-run prints the plan and runs each step's own dry run, nothing written; everything after -- goes to the one --only step as its switches. New (CLI arc phase 1, the switches and the dry run phase 4); section 7.0.
    update --scheduledThe scheduled pass itself (what schedule on registers; the former pass verb of the sync noun): the same update under the no-terminal rules, the tidy stage by threshold.
    schedule on / uninstallRegister the pass with the platform scheduler, or remove it.
    schedule status / pause / resumeIs it installed, is it paused, when did it last run; every docenta job on the machine with its store and its command.
    layers stopEnd the semantic pipeline running on this store now, one an import started included; every layer keeps its cursor and the next run continues from there (schedule stop ends an update pass).
    schedule migrate [--dry-run] [--json]Rewrite every docenta job on this machine that still spells the pass verb an older build wrote to update --scheduled, keeping its store flags, cadence, paths and priority; docenta setup update runs it after every swap. --dry-run prints the old and new command lines and changes nothing. New (CLI arc phase 4); section 7.2.

    bale - moving a store

    CommandPurpose
    store export ROOTList what the store holds under ROOT; --select/--all exports it as one signed, sealed file.
    store import FILELand a bale under /@<origin>/; a second import of the same origin replaces what the first landed under the same roots (instances and locked vector segments alike), and leaves the origin's other roots as they are.
    store inspect FILEWhat a bale holds, without landing it (--verify streams every member); with a store here, what its vectors would do on import: the partitions this store has, the ones it lacks, and the ones the landing would create.
    store land [BALE]Take in the vector segments an import deferred (the model not installed then, a pipeline holding the store), without the bale file and without verifying it again; the gate is asked again, the partition is created when the same model is installed here.
    store imports / store forget-import LABELThe origins imported here with every locked vector segment (the bale and roots it came in, where and when it was cut), and the retirement of one.

    tidy - space back and the store in top shape

    CommandPurpose
    tidy [--only gc|compact|semantic-compact|expire] [--force-wave] [--no-reconcile] [--repair] [--resume] [--hold-days N] [--collapse-alias-paths]The reclaim below with the semantic stack once more after the compaction and the final check of every layer; --force-wave is the one reviewed acceptance of both breakers (gc's mass-orphan limit, the semantic removal wave). New (CLI arc phase 1); section 8.0.
    tidy (the whole reclaim)Reconcile, drop, and return the space - the whole sequence. The reconcile is a full walk of the roots the store owns, decided before anything is changed: a named store's store.toml roots, else the roots its ingests recorded (ingest folder DIR, an onboarding folder), else, for this machine's own store only, every fixed drive. A --data-dir store that recorded no roots, or only the whole machine, is refused with nothing changed, --repair included: record its folder with ingest folder DIR, or run tidy --no-reconcile. A recorded root that is not there now is named and not walked. The walk is followed by a look at every file row it did not reach: a folder that MOVED to another disk is walked at its new place only, so its old rows are put to the disk here and retired when their files are gone from a volume that is attached. An unplugged drive retires nothing. What it removes reaches the semantic layers in the same run (docenta update --only prune), before anything is compacted, and what the walk re-read (files that changed since the last pass) is indexed in the same run too (docenta-semantic pipeline), so search ends current and no later pass is left to finish it.
    tidy --only compact [--repair] [--resume]Recompress, vacuum, force-merge (the former store verb of that name); --repair for dangling references.
    tidy --only gc [--collapse-alias-paths]Drop derivatives of deleted files (the former store verb of that name).
    tidy --only expire [--hold-days N]End the absence hold now (the former store verb of that name).
    tidy --only semantic-compactThe semantic sibling's compaction alone.

    store - the store's lifecycle

    CommandPurpose
    store initCreate the layout and apply migrations. Idempotent.
    store verifyProve stored text matches disk.
    store backup --to DIR [--no-blobs]A consistent backup while docenta runs: the catalog and the license databases by SQLite's online backup, each copy checked, the config and license files, then the blobs incrementally.
    store check [FILE]Check the catalog, or a backup's copy, with docenta's path collation (the system's sqlite3 cannot read its indexes).
    store identity [--label LABEL] [--public-key]This store's node id, label, and device key (the former setup verb).
    store paths [--drive LETTER]Every live path, one per line (the former corpus verb).
    store forget PREFIXRetire a subtree deliberately.
    store resetDelete every derived store (never your files or models).
    docenta-gateway --data-dir DIR --listen ADDRThe door: serves one store's MCP tools over HTTP for remote clients (bearer from DOCENTA_GATEWAY_TOKEN; TLS is the proxy's job). A separate binary: docenta itself never opens a socket. Several stores behind one brain: --store NAME=DIR (repeatable) and --host HOST=NAME route by hostname.
    serve --stores NAME=DIR ...Several stores from one process: every tool takes store, the model workers are shared.
    agents add [--client claude-code|codex|cursor|chatgpt|all] [--door URL] [--enforce] [--dry-run] [--yes]Connect the agents on this machine to docenta, deliberately: each client found is explained (the server, the standing DOCENTA FIRST rule, the pre-compaction hook, the re-ground after a compaction), asked, written, and the connection proven with one handshake and one search. Claude Code, Codex (CLI, IDE, ChatGPT desktop), Cursor; ChatGPT on the web gets the words to paste. A docenta entry you wrote by hand is merged into, never declared a second time: in Codex's config.toml a [mcp_servers.docenta] table outside the docenta markers is adopted into the block, your own keys (env, enabled, extra args, a timeout you set) kept under the # docenta:kept line, and an approval table for a tool docenta no longer serves dropped; --dry-run names each. A Codex config that does not parse, before or after the change, is refused and left untouched, and the proof parses the written file the way Codex does. The Codex table carries docenta's own startup_timeout_sec = 60 and tool_timeout_sec = 300 unless you set your own (Codex's defaults are 10 and 60: ten seconds was the field failure of 2026-10-09 on a large store before the handshake was answered first, and the first call after a cold start waits for the store to open; the sixty cover a machine under load and a shim that serves without a hub endpoint). Claude Code has no per-server startup knob (its MCP_TIMEOUT, 30 s by default, is the client's own environment) and Cursor documents none, so setup writes nothing of the kind for them. Re-running changes nothing. Onboarding runs it once; run it again on an older store or after a new client lands. --refresh-installed rewrites only the clients whose configs already carry docenta's entry (the server key or docenta's markers), without a question, and checks each written file; it never adds a client, and docenta-setup update runs it after every update.
    agents add --profile NAME [--page-budget CHARS] [--client ...]A second registration of the same store for one serving profile: --profile memory writes the server docenta-memory beside docenta for Claude Code, Cursor and Codex, started as docenta serve --profile memory, so an agent that only does memory never passes the argument. Only the server entry is written (the rule file and the hooks are the plain run's). agents refresh keeps it pointed at the binary; uninstall agents removes it.
    store ship NAME --root DIR [--public DIR] [--title TEXT] [--describe TEXT] [--cut full|public] [-o FILE] [--plain | --to KEY] [--trust-folders] [--no-sizing]A pile of data to a sealed bale in one command: the store is made NAME.docenta-store beside the data and registered (when new), the data is ingested, the semantic stack runs end to end (--embed/--sparse decide up front), the store is sealed with its card once every layer is current, and the bale of the chosen cut is exported. The sealed store beside the data is what door/build.sh NAME=DIR@HOST puts in the cloud; the bale is what another machine imports (store import FILE --as NAME). This is the ADU flow of 2026-09-12 (~/ADU/store beside ~/ADU/codes, sealed, bales in ~/ADU/bales, the door from the sealed store), wired as one verb. The first step SIZES the whole before anything is spent: files, the read time, units, local hours and GPU-hours, and the store's size against the free space of its volume; a volume that cannot hold the store is refused (--no-sizing skips the step). --trust-folders re-walks by folders, so an interrupted ship resumes where it stopped.
    store new NAME --root DIR [--public DIR] [--at DATA_DIR] [--title TEXT] [--describe TEXT] / store listA NAMED STORE: a specialist collection with its own file of record (store.toml: the name, the title the collection is called by when that is not the store's name, the roots with their rights class, a self-contained layout), registered under its name so every verb takes --store NAME instead of --data-dir and a config. --public DIR declares a root the PUBLIC cut may carry; store export --cut public then selects exactly those, and store import --as NAME lands the bale as a named store on the other machine. The privacy crumb goes on every root so the machine's own store never sweeps it.
    store seal --reason TEXT --name NAME --describe TEXT / store unsealFreeze the content (searches keep answering; ingest, sync, gc, reclaim, forget, reset, enrich, bale import are refused until unsealed) and record the corpus card the MCP server shows first. On a named store the card's words are kept in store.toml (title, description), so a rebuild that lifts the seal and ships again by name keeps what the collection is called; store unseal hands an older seal's words over the same way. For a collection served to others; serve it as its own MCP server with docenta serve --data-dir DIR.
    store hold --reason TEXT / store releaseStop every semantic step on this one store until released: the pipeline, cloud ship and store ship refuse with the reason, content may still come in, and docenta status --content says first that the store is held. For a collection whose scope, disk or GPU budget is not decided yet.

    setup - who, what, where

    CommandPurpose
    setup onboardThe one onboarding command.
    setup estimate [--root DIR | --preset NAME] [--json]Probe the machine, classify it, estimate a scope before anything starts (the former preflight).
    setup configEvery resolved path and what decided it.
    setup answers [--set KEY=WORD]... [--reset] [--json]Show, ask, set and reset the answers (ocr, mbox, mail, agents, chats, embed, json): the ledger, the lane word, the consent, the config's two choices; writes records only and says what applies them. New (CLI arc phase 1); section 7.0.2.
    setup licenseThe license state and its remedy (the same report as license status); a machine not on Pro is pointed at docenta shop.

    why - the inclusion policy's verdict

    CommandPurpose
    why PATHWhy a path is, or is not, in the corpus: the rule that decided, an external root's origin, whether the store holds it today (the former corpus verb).

    dev - the instruments (hidden from docenta --help; docenta dev --help lists them)

    CommandPurpose
    dev probe search|dense|hybrid|expand ...One retrieval channel queried directly (docenta-semantic dev probe).
    dev bench qrels|dense|quant|embed|sparse|graph|golden|agent-eval|coverage|evidence ...The measurement rigs (docenta-semantic dev bench).
    dev embed ...The embed arm with every knob (docenta-semantic dev embed).
    dev turbo keygen|seal|open|ops|pack|pack-model|split|run-local|import|verify|parity|providers|sparse|work|drive ...The operator's and the fleet's side of the cloud lane (docenta-semantic dev turbo).
    dev uffsAccelerated ingest on Windows NTFS volumes, by hand with its knobs (ingest machine rides it by itself where it applies).
    dev enumerate --root DIR --out FILEWrite a work list to a file for a later ingest manifest.
    dev original CONTENT_ID [--out FILE]The bytes a content id was read from, verified against the id before one is served (a mailbox member or an attachment is re-derived from its container). A check of the ingestion pipeline: what a lane read, held against what it extracted.
    dev layoutEvery path the system uses, as JSON, for scripts (the former setup verb).
    dev families [--json]The content families of the modality ladder and their extensions (the former setup verb).
    dev replay LOGReplay a query log against the current engine and measure what changed.
    dev usn-scan --root VOLUMERead the NTFS USN change journal for a volume in isolation.

    layers calibrate - the fusion table, judged by what agents read

    CommandPurpose
    layers calibrateThe status page of this store's calibration: what is in force, what the query log holds, what is still missing (the former top-level verb; answered by docenta itself, the query log is its own).
    layers calibrate --applyAdopt the winning table when the evidence clears the bar.
    layers calibrate --resetReturn to the shipped constants.

    Calibration is opt-in and local. It reads the query log this machine wrote, replays it offline against candidate fusion tables, and adopts one only when the evidence clears a bar it names. Nothing is sent anywhere, and --reset puts the shipped constants back.

    layers model - the dense model a store embeds under

    CommandPurpose
    layers modelThe installed models, each with its partition's share of the feed, which one is configured (the knob or the default order) and which one serves the queries (answered by docenta itself: the knob lives in its config file). --json for a tool.
    layers model NAMESet [storage] production_embedder to NAME. The embed step builds its partition from the next pass (docenta cloud ship sends it to the GPU lane); the queries keep their built partition meanwhile and move at the next mount once the new one is built. Refused, without --anyway, when the serving partition is itself below the built line and the switch would leave the meaning channel to the lazy path.
    layers model --defaultRemove the knob; the default order picks the model again.

    The verb replaces the config line typed by hand (the runbook docs/runbooks/dense-model-upgrade.md has the staged upgrade); nothing is retired by it, layers partitions does that.

    docenta-semantic - the meaning layer#

    Reached as docenta layers <verb>, docenta cloud <verb> and docenta ask (CLI arc phase 2): docenta finds the program in its own install (beside itself, or in the helpers folder below it), passes --data-dir and --store through, inherits the terminal, forwards Ctrl-C and a kill, and ends with the sibling's exit code. Since the arc's third phase (2026-10-09) the sibling's own page lists only what a person reaches through docenta: status, pipeline, runtime, graph, reset, partitions, models and cloud status | receive | retry | consent HOURS | ship | estimate; answer is docenta ask, the instruments (probe, bench, embed) and the operator's and the fleet's turbo verbs are docenta dev ... (docenta dev --help lists them), and the semantic compaction, prune and repair are steps of docenta tidy and docenta update. docenta setup runtime is docenta-semantic runtime, docenta setup models is docenta-semantic models.

    CommandPurpose
    pipelineRun all eight layers in order. The one command you need.
    status [--watch|--exact]Per-layer build state. --watch to follow. The pending units are counted on the feed tail when the tail is short; a long tail shows the count the last pipeline took, with its age, and --exact counts it now (minutes on a large backlog: it reads every bundle the tail adds).
    index / embedRun one layer by itself.
    search / dense / hybridUnit keyword / meaning / fused search.
    answerAssemble one evidence pack with an enforced token budget.
    entities / claims / communities / modulesThe understanding layers.
    goldenRun judged questions as a regression gate.
    compact / compact-vectorsMerge segments, rewrite vectors, rebuild the query snapshot.
    resetDelete the semantic layer (--units, --vectors).
    setup models --moveMove the model store safely.
    layers focus add PATH [--weight W] / layers focus listThe focus ledger: pin a tree so the background walk embeds its neighbourhood first; the decayed scoreboard. Answered by docenta itself (the ledger lives there), reached under semantic (the former corpus verb).
    cloud ship / cloud statusPack the semantic lanes for a rented GPU when no pack stands - sparse, dense and, when the code model is installed and code units are pending, the code lane (the qwen3 partition over the code_symbol units, since 2026-10-09) - quote every lane, ask within the consent, seal and send the pack to the relay (one verb: the former prep, pack, quotes and ship); see where every job stands, in the relay's count: shards landed of shards sent, pods on it, and for a job that came back short the shards that did not finish with their reason and the cloud retry command that puts them back.
    cloud retry [--job ID]The second path when the fleet's own retries left shards behind (owner 2026-10-17): the same job queued again for exactly the shards without a result - the sealed inputs are still on the relay, nothing is packed or uploaded twice, what landed stays home and is neither run nor charged again. Without --job it takes the one failed or partial job of this store and names them when there are several. The record goes back to open and the lanes with shards out are marked out again, so the next pass waits for the results instead of shipping the rest a second time; cloud receive brings them home when they land (the hourly pass does so on its own). The fleet's first line of its own: a shard is tried three times, a host that has not booted within twice the measured mean boot is replaced, and a lane that has booted never spends its shards over slow hosts.
    cloud estimateCount the three pending lanes - sparse texts, dense units, code units - the way the pack counts them (minutes) and quote them on every provider card, each lane in its own column: the card's measured rate, or "not measured" (never a number inferred from another lane's rate); the local row is this machine's measured rates, or "not measured" until a pass has run; the last line is the relay's own quote for the shape, the GPU-hours cloud ship asks you to consent to. --quick projects the dense lane alone from a sample in seconds and says so; --dir DIR quotes a written pack.
    cloud shop (docenta cloud shop)The shop with the GPU-hours first: packs of whole GPU-hours (5, 10, 25, 50, priced from the rate card at the overage multiplier), paid on the site and credited here for the next jobs; Pro is on the same page. docenta shop is the same page with everything, docenta license with Pro first; cloud ship sends the person there with the job's shortfall when nothing else funds it.
    cloud consent HOURS (docenta cloud consent HOURS)Your word with the number and no job quoted: the standing consent a pass with nobody at a terminal ships under. A new consent replaces the standing one and counts from zero; 0 withdraws it.
    bench-*Measurement harnesses (throughput, recall, quantization).

    Three lanes under one word. The code partition (qwen3-embedding-0.6b over the code_symbol units, the hybrid's code-dense channel) is the third lane since 2026-10-09: the one lane word covers all three (turbo ships them, local builds them, lazy and later leave them), no new question is asked at the onboarding, and the sizing page, the site's decision, the quote, the consent, the ship, the receive, docenta status and docenta layers status all carry the code lane with its own count, rate and time. A machine without the code model installed says so on the page and skips the lane. The status page's code line is the partition's pending count by count (the index's code_symbol units less the vectors held), the lane's turbo work when any is out, and "no code model installed" otherwise.

    The turbo consent and its ceiling. The word turbo stands for the store: a later refresh that finds a delta over the line packs it and sends it on that word, with nobody at a terminal. What it may send is capped by the quote you said yes to. The consent is recorded with its GPU-hours and the job's text, unit and code unit counts when you say yes with the numbers on the screen (at the onboarding, at cloud consent <hours>, at cloud ship --consent <hours>, or with --yes typed at a terminal), every shipped job's quote is spent against it, and a pass with nobody at a terminal (the hourly sync, the onboarding's detached build) ships only a job that fits inside what is left plus a small allowance for ordinary growth between passes: a tenth of the consent, at least 0.1 GPU-hours, and spent like the rest so an hourly trickle cannot add up past it. A job beyond that is not sent and nothing is rented: the pass prints one line with the quote, the consented figure, what is left and the exact command that consents to the new amount (docenta cloud ship --consent <hours>, or docenta cloud consent <hours> for the ceiling alone), raises the desktop notification, and leaves the pack for your word. At a terminal the same job is one question with the numbers, default no. status and cloud status show the standing consent and what is left of it. A new consent replaces the standing one and counts from zero.

    docenta-spool - connectors#

    CommandPurpose
    chatsRender AI chats, then ingest them.
    gitRender every repository's history (the delta since the recorded tips), then ingest it.
    claude / openaiOne chat connector at a time.
    imapFetch new mail over IMAPS using an app password.

    docenta-analysis - the OCR producer#

    docenta update --only produce

    The update's produce step. The producer is code in docenta, started as a process of its own with --analysis-root DIR --state-db FILE --models DIR [--limit N]. Long-running and safe to stop; re-running skips work already done. docenta update --only analysis makes the results searchable.

    It reads pictures (images, and PDFs with no real text layer) and, since 2026-09-12, PDFs whose text layer is all there but in the wrong order (a plan sheet, a form, a map laid out by column): docenta judges that at ingest and records the verdict on the content object, the producer re-reads those pages, and a hit served from OCR text says extraction: ocr. A store ingested before the verdict existed gets it filled in by docenta update --only enrich -- --only verdicts (it reads the stored text, never the originals).

    12. The pages docenta shows you#

    docenta is a terminal tool, but a few things read better as a page than as a wall of text: a plan you are about to approve, the book you are reading now, the four steps of a mail login. This chapter names every page docenta or one of its siblings can put in front of you, so none of them is a surprise.

    12.1 The rule#

    If this machine can show a page, you get the page. If it cannot, you get the same thing as text. Nothing is hidden behind a window that never opens. docenta measures the machine rather than assuming: an explicit DOCENTA_BROWSER=never or always settles it, otherwise macOS and Windows always have an opener, and a Unix box needs a graphical session (DISPLAY or WAYLAND_DISPLAY) with xdg-open on the path. A container, a build agent or an ssh login without forwarding is told which of those it lacks, and gets the text.

    A page that lives on this computer never sends anything anywhere: it explains, or it asks and hands your answers to the terminal that opened it. A page that asks never decides for you: every question starts not set with its default marked, the submit points at the first one still open and refuses until all are answered, the "answered" tag on a question unsets it, and what you answered is kept in this browser until it is handed over, so a crash loses nothing (a password is never kept). Where the terminal takes a typed word - the removal and the reset - the page explains and the terminal decides. A page on the site decides only what it says it decides, and you reach it by a link or a short code the terminal prints, never by docenta opening an address on its own.

    Every page carries the same bar: the text size (minus, the percent, plus; steps from 85 to 200; Command or Control with plus, minus and 0 on the page itself, the browser's own zoom untouched; remembered in this browser for every docenta page), and the theme (system, light, dark; its tooltip names the active one and the next). A table wider than the text takes the screen's width, centered, before it takes a scrollbar.

    12.2 The catalogue#

    PageWhat makes itWhere it livesWhat it decides
    The start pagean early-access invitation mailthe site, behind a link that is yoursnothing; the install steps and how to connect your assistant to your desk's collection
    The sign-in and approval pagesan assistant you are connecting to a hosted collectionthe site; they open by themselveswho you are (your address and six digits) and, with one button, whether that assistant may ask that collection
    The confirmation pagethe mail sent when you ask for early accessthe site; its one button poststhat the address is yours, which is what lets the desk see your question
    The onboarding questionsdocenta setup onboarda listener on this computer only, on 127.0.0.1every up-front answer: OCR, the mailbox archives, a mail account, the agents; the terminal continues on the submit
    The mail setup pagedocenta setup maila listener on this computer only, on 127.0.0.1which mailbox and which key; the key goes to the OS credential store, never a file
    The sizing decisiondocenta setup onboardthe site, reached with a short code the terminal printswhether the semantic build runs here, on turbo, or later
    The turbo price carddocenta cloud shipthe sitenothing; it states what a job of that shape costs
    The payment pagea turbo job that needs fundingthe site, at a link the terminal printswhether the job is funded
    The removal plandocenta uninstall --pagea file on this computer, opened from disknothing; the typed confirmation stays in the terminal
    The reset plandocenta store reset --pagea file on this computer, opened from disknothing; the typed confirmation stays in the terminal
    This handbookdocenta handbooka file beside the binariesnothing

    12.3 Seeing them for yourself#

    docenta handbook --samples ~/docenta-pages

    writes one example of every page this binary renders, plus an index describing the whole catalogue above, and opens the index. The samples are drawn by the same code the real commands call, from one example machine, so they cannot drift from what you will actually see.

    12.4 This handbook, in two forms#

    Every install carries both: HANDBOOK.md for reading anywhere, and HANDBOOK.html for reading in a browser, with the glossary live - every term you meet is underlined, says what it means when you rest on it, jumps to its entry when you click it, and every entry has a "back" that returns you to exactly the place you were reading.

    docenta handbook picks the form your machine can show and says which it chose and why. docenta handbook --print always writes the text to your terminal.

    The words in this book#

    Each dotted word in the chapters shows its meaning when you rest on it and jumps here when you click it. Every entry has a back that returns you to the line you were reading.

    Agentback
    an AI assistant that can use tools for you, such as Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor. docenta is one of the tools it can use: the agent asks, docenta finds the page.
    App passwordback
    a separate password your mail provider makes for one program only. Your real password stays yours, and you can throw the app password away at any time.
    Backgroundback
    work that keeps going on its own after the command returns. You can close the window; it continues.
    Baleback
    a packed box of what docenta learned, made for carrying to another of your own machines. Every item inside is listed with its fingerprint, so a box that was opened or changed on the way is refused.
    Binaryback
    a program file the computer can run. docenta is eight of them, all in one folder.
    Bundleback
    docenta's written record of one file it read: what it found inside and when. The meaning layers read these records to learn what is new.
    Cacheback
    a saved copy of an answer, kept so the same work is not done twice.
    Citationback
    the exact file, page or line an answer came from, so you can open it and check.
    Claimsback
    small facts docenta noted while reading, such as who did what and when. Timelines are built from them.
    CLIback
    short for command line interface: using a program by typing in the terminal instead of clicking.
    Commandback
    a line you type in the terminal and finish with the Enter key. Everything this book shows in a grey box is one.
    Commitback
    one saved step in a git history, with a note saying what changed and why.
    Compactionback
    tidying the store so it takes less room, like closing the gaps on a bookshelf. docenta does it by itself after a big read.
    Content idback
    the name docenta gives a piece of content: the word blake3: followed by its fingerprint. It names what the content IS, not where it lives, so it stays the same when a file moves.
    Content objectback
    one distinct piece of content. Ten copies of the same photo are ten files but one content object, so docenta reads it once.
    Corpusback
    everything docenta has read for you, taken together: your files, your mail, your chats, your code history. When this book says "18 percent of the corpus" it means 18 percent of all of that, measured in bytes on your disk.
    Cursorback
    a bookmark. Each part of docenta writes down how far it got, so after a stop it carries on from there instead of starting over.
    Dense vectorsback
    the long lists of numbers a model writes for each passage, used to find text by meaning. See vector.
    Doorback
    a collection we host so your assistant can ask it over the internet. It is the only thing that lives on our side; your own files never do.
    Drop box
    a folder, ~/.docenta/drops/<provider>, where you put a download docenta cannot fetch for you, such as a chat export.
    Embedderback
    the model that turns a passage of text into its list of numbers.
    Entityback
    a person, a company, a place or an account that docenta recognises as the same one across many files.
    Evidence packback
    one ready-made briefing for your assistant: the passages that answer the question, where each came from, where sources disagree, and what could not be found. It is kept short on purpose.
    Extractionback
    pulling the words out of a file, whatever kind it is: a PDF, a Word file, an email, a photo of a page.
    Familyback
    the kind of thing a file is: text, document, image, animated, media, archive or unknown. Each kind except unknown has its own reader.
    File instanceback
    one place on your disk where a piece of content was found. Many instances of few content objects means you keep many copies.
    Fingerprintback
    a short code worked out from a file's contents, also called a hash or a checksum. Change one letter and the code changes, so two files with the same fingerprint are the same file.
    Flagback
    an extra word on a command that starts with two dashes, like --json. It changes how the command behaves.
    Full Disk Accessback
    a macOS permission that lets a program read all your folders without the system asking folder by folder.
    Gazetteerback
    docenta's list of names and their spellings, so that "Bob Smith" and "Robert Smith" are understood as one person.
    Gitback
    a tool programmers use to keep every past version of their files, with a note for each change.
    GPUback
    the chip that draws pictures on a screen. It is also very fast at the arithmetic the models need.
    Ignore fileback
    a file named .docentaignore that lists what docenta must not read, one pattern per line.
    IMAPback
    the standard way a program reads mail from a mail provider such as Gmail, iCloud or Yahoo.
    Indexback
    a list of every word and where it appears, like the index at the back of a book, so a question is answered in a blink.
    Ingestback
    reading every file once and writing what it says into the index. It is the long part of the first run, and it resumes if stopped.
    JSONback
    a tidy text format that programs read easily. Add --json to a command and it answers in it.
    Keyword searchback
    finding the exact words you typed, like the search box you already know. Also called lexical search.
    Laneback
    the reader for one family of files: one lane reads documents, another reads images. Each lane has a version number, and when it improves docenta re-reads that family by itself.
    Leaseback
    a signed permission file, tied to one machine, that says which edition of docenta may run on it.
    Lock fileback
    a small file that says "someone is working here", so two runs cannot trip over each other.
    Mboxback
    one big file holding many emails, the form mail downloads come in.
    MCPback
    the standard plug that lets your assistant ask docenta questions. One plug, and every assistant fits. The letters stand for Model Context Protocol.
    Mentionback
    one place where a person's or a company's name appears in your files.
    Metadataback
    facts about a file rather than what it says: its name, its size, its dates.
    Migrationback
    a one-time change to the layout of the store when docenta is upgraded. It happens by itself.
    Modelback
    a file that turns words into numbers, so the computer can tell that "car" and "automobile" mean nearly the same thing. It runs on your machine and is never sent anywhere.
    OAuth
    letting your mail provider hand docenta a permission of its own, with no password copied anywhere. "Sign in with Google" is this.
    OCRback
    reading the words in a picture or a scanned page, the way you can read a photo of a sign. The letters stand for optical character recognition.
    ONNX Runtimeback
    a helper program from Microsoft that lets the models run on your own computer's chips. Fetched once.
    Originalsback
    your own files. docenta reads them and never copies, moves or changes them.
    Partitionback
    one shelf of vectors, all written by the same model. A different model gets its own shelf, because numbers from two models cannot be compared.
    PATHback
    the list of folders your terminal looks in when you type a program's name. Once docenta's folder is on it, typing docenta just works.
    Pipelineback
    the steps that build the meaning layers, run one after another in a fixed order. Each step picks up where it stopped.
    Placeholderback
    a file that only pretends to be on your disk: its contents live in a cloud drive until you open it. docenta cannot read what is not there.
    Preflightback
    the quick estimate before a long job: how much there is to do, how long it will take and how much disk it needs.
    Recipeback
    the exact way a piece of extracted text was made: which reader, which version, which model. When the recipe changes, docenta makes it again.
    Reclaimback
    removing from the store what belonged to files that are gone or that you excluded.
    Reindexback
    building the index again from what docenta already extracted, without reading your files again.
    Repositoryback
    a folder whose whole history git keeps.
    Rerankerback
    a last careful reader that takes the best few answers and puts them in the right order.
    Rust
    the programming language docenta is written in. You never need it: docenta reaches you already built.
    Scanback
    a quick look for what changed since last time, so only new or changed files are read again.
    Schedulerback
    the part of your computer that starts a program at set times. On macOS it is launchd, on Windows Task Scheduler, on Linux cron.
    Schemaback
    the layout of the tables inside the store: which facts are kept and in which columns.
    Sealback
    freezing a collection, so that nothing is added, changed or removed afterwards.
    Semantic searchback
    the part that understands meaning, not just spelling: ask about "the roof leak" and it finds the mail that said "water coming through the ceiling". The semantic layers are built after the index, in the background.
    Sidecar / blobback
    the words docenta pulled out of a file, squeezed small and kept in the store. It is never the file itself.
    Signedback
    carrying a signature from us that your computer can check, so a file that was changed or swapped on the way is refused.
    Snippetback
    the few lines around a match, shown so you can see why it matched.
    Sparse termsback
    a second word list a model writes for each passage, adding related words the text did not literally use. It helps a keyword find text that says the same thing differently.
    Spoolback
    a folder, ~/.docenta/spool, where the connectors write your mail and chats as ordinary files. docenta then reads them like any other file.
    Stdioback
    the simplest way two programs on one computer talk: one writes lines, the other reads them. Nothing goes over the network.
    Storeback
    the folder where docenta keeps what it learned about your files. Your files themselves are never copied or moved.
    Syncback
    one pass that brings everything up to date: new files, new mail, new chats.
    Takeoutback
    Google's download of everything in your account, mail included.
    Terminalback
    the window where you type commands instead of clicking. On a Mac it is the app called Terminal; on Windows it is PowerShell.
    Themeback
    a topic that runs across many of your files, found by docenta on its own. Also called a community.
    Timelineback
    what happened, in order, with the file behind each step.
    Tokenback
    a piece of a word, the unit AI assistants count when they read. Fewer tokens means a faster and cheaper answer, which is why docenta hands over the right passage and not the whole file.
    Turboback
    renting a GPU for a few hours so the slow arithmetic finishes in hours instead of days. Only the extracted text travels, sealed, and the rented machine is destroyed afterwards. Three lanes ride it: the sparse terms, the dense vectors and, since 2026-10-09, the code partition's vectors.
    Unitback
    a passage-sized piece of a document. It is what the meaning layers index and cite, so an answer points at a paragraph and not at a whole file.
    Vectorback
    the list of numbers a model makes from a piece of text, also called an embedding. Texts that mean similar things get similar numbers, which is how a search by meaning works.
    WAL
    short for write-ahead log: a notebook the store writes into first, so nothing is lost if the power fails halfway through a write.
    This book ships with the binaries. docenta handbook opens it on your own machine, docenta handbook --print writes the text to your terminal, and HANDBOOK.md beside it is the same book as text.
